items.title: Trump administration pauses all US visa applications worldwide
items.description: The United States has paused immigrant visa applications as the Donald Trump administration moves to tighten screening and limit entry for applicants considered likely to depend on government assistance. A US State Department official confirmed the development on Tuesday, saying the initiative was launched at American embassies and consulates in early August, per report by The Guardian UK. The department said visa appointments had to be adjusted to accommodate “in-depth training” for consular officers as part of efforts to strengthen the assessment of applicants. The State Department has been working on updated guidance and training since early this year, the official said, “to ensure all consular officers are fully equipped to evaluate every visa applicant comprehensively and consistently”. Applicants who had already secured interview appointments were reportedly informed by email that their appointments had been cancelled and that they would be notified of new dates. The move is intended to ensure that immigrants do not become reliant on US public benefits, according to agency officials. It is also part of a broader immigration crackdown by the Trump administration targeting both lawful and undocumented immigration. The latest development comes amid several other measures introduced by the administration to tighten access to the United States. This week, the Trump administration announced plans to revoke visas from some asylum seekers who initially entered the US on tourist or business visas. Up to 200,000 people currently seeking asylum could be affected by the move, which would potentially become the largest mass visa revocation exercise in US history. The action is being carried out in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security. Visa applicants have also faced additional requirements under Trump, including scrutiny of their social media histories and increased processing costs. The immigrant visa pause follows an earlier attempt by the Trump administration to restrict applications on a similar “public charge” basis. That policy included a suspension of immigrant visa processing for applicants from 75 countries, but a federal judge recently overturned the measure. Reacting to the ruling, Joanna Cuevas Ingram, senior staff attorney at the National Immigration Law Center, said: “The court made clear that immigration laws cannot be used to justify discrimination,” She added: “We are determined to ensure every person and family this ban harmed receives appropriate relief and will continue to hold this administration accountable to its obligations under the law.” The latest visa restrictions are expected to create further difficulties for applicants who have already spent significant amounts of money and made travel arrangements for interviews. Brian Simmons, an attorney at immigration law firm Fragomen in Washington, told the Financial Times that many applicants affected by the pause likely “spent thousands of dollars and disrupted their lives to attend scheduled interviews, only to have their appointments cancelled at the last minute”. It remains unclear when the cancelled appointments will be rescheduled, leaving many applicants facing further uncertainty over their immigration plans. The development comes as the Trump administration continues to introduce stricter immigration policies, several of which have faced legal challenges in US courts. items.title: UBA discloses delay in release of H1’26 financial statements
items.description: By Chukwunonso Okolo United Bank for Africa Plc, has informed shareholders and the investing public of a potential delay in the publication of its Audited Financial Statements (AFS) for the first half 2026, H1 ‘26, ended 30 June, as required by the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) listing rules. This was disclosed by the Bank in a statement signed by Bili A. Odum , the Group’s company secretary/legal counsel. According to the statement, the Group’s Audited Accounts and Financial Statements for the first half 2026, H1’26, was considered and approved by the Board of Directors of United Bank for Africa Plc at its meeting held on August 13, 2026. “However, the approval of the Central Bank of Nigeria is required before the release of the results, Odun added. “ In this regard, the United Bank for Africa Plc has requested and obtained approval of the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX) for an extension of time to file the Results on or before September 30, 2026, subject to obtaining the requisite regulatory approvals for the publication of its Audited Financial Statements (AFS). “The Bank’s insiders are hereby reminded that the previously declared Closed Period in respect of transactions in the Bank’s securities remains in effect until twenty-four (24) hours after the publication of the Results,” the statement noted. items.title: Dumping : Rabat taxe les importations de panneaux de bois en provenance de Chine et d’Indonésie
items.description: Le Maroc a décidé d’appliquer des droits antidumping provisoires sur les importations de panneaux de bois à âme épaisse en provenance de Chine et d’Indonésie, à l’issue d’une enquête ouverte sur de présumées pratiques de dumping affectant le marché national. Les mesures annoncées prévoient un droit de 82 % pour les producteurs-exportateurs chinois et de 55 % pour leurs homologues indonésiens. Selon l’avis DDC/11/2026, cette décision s’inscrit dans le cadre des mécanismes de régulation du commerce extérieur et de préservation d’une concurrence jugée équitable. Elle reflète également la volonté des autorités marocaines de mobiliser les dispositions de la loi n°15.09 relative aux mesures de défense commerciale afin de protéger l’industrie nationale contre les pratiques considérées comme préjudiciables. Le document, consulté par Hespress , précise qu’aucun producteur-exportateur chinois ou indonésien de panneaux de bois à âme épaisse n’a participé à l’enquête antidumping. En l’absence de coopération des entreprises concernées, les conclusions ont été établies sur la base des « meilleures informations disponibles », conformément aux règles prévues par l’Accord antidumping de l’Organisation mondiale du commerce ainsi que par la législation marocaine en vigueur. Pour mener son analyse, le ministère de l’Industrie et du Commerce s’est appuyé sur les données contenues dans la plainte ayant déclenché la procédure, mais également sur les informations issues de la plateforme PORTNET , guichet unique dédié à la simplification des opérations de commerce extérieur au Maroc, ainsi que sur les statistiques de l’Office des changes. Ces éléments ont servi de référence en remplacement des données qui auraient dû être fournies par les exportateurs concernés. L’enquête a retenu comme valeur normale la moyenne des factures de vente sur le marché intérieur chinois ainsi que des offres de vente appliquées sur le marché domestique indonésien. Ces références ont ensuite été comparées aux prix pratiqués à l’exportation vers le Maroc afin de mesurer l’ampleur des écarts de prix. Les prix à l’exportation des fabricants chinois et indonésiens ont, pour leur part, été calculés à partir des factures de vente destinées au marché marocain, au stade commercial « départ usine » (Ex-Factory), en tenant compte des ajustements jugés nécessaires dans le cadre de l’enquête. Les résultats de cette comparaison ont fait apparaître des marges de dumping particulièrement élevées. Celles-ci ont été évaluées à 147,42 % du prix à l’exportation pour les producteurs-exportateurs chinois et à 140,21 % pour les producteurs-exportateurs indonésiens. Des niveaux qui, selon les conclusions préliminaires de l’enquête, traduisent un écart significatif entre les prix pratiqués sur les marchés de référence et ceux appliqués à l’export vers le Maroc. Au-delà de la question des prix, les autorités ont examiné l’impact économique de ces importations sur l’industrie nationale. L’analyse met en évidence une hausse notable des volumes importés de panneaux de bois à âme épaisse en provenance de Chine et d’Indonésie durant la période couverte par l’enquête, aussi bien en termes absolus qu’au regard de la production et de la consommation nationales. Le rapport souligne également que ces importations ont exercé une pression significative sur les prix du produit fabriqué localement. L’enquête a notamment relevé un phénomène de sous-cotation persistante, les produits importés étant proposés à des prix inférieurs à ceux des fabricants marocains tout au long de la période examinée. Cette situation aurait contribué à maintenir une pression continue sur les niveaux de prix observés sur le marché intérieur. Les indicateurs relatifs à la branche de production nationale font par ailleurs état d’une dégradation de plusieurs paramètres économiques durant la période sous examen. Les autorités y voient la manifestation d’un « dommage important » affectant l’industrie locale et fragilisant sa position face à la concurrence étrangère. À la lumière de ces constats, le ministère de l’Industrie et du Commerce considère, à titre préliminaire, que la branche de production nationale a subi un préjudice important au sens de l’article 13 de la loi n°15.09 relative aux mesures de défense commerciale. Le rapport estime également que cette branche demeure « très vulnérable » face aux importations faisant l’objet de dumping en provenance de Chine et d’Indonésie. Sur le plan juridique, les enquêteurs indiquent avoir établi l’existence d’un lien de causalité entre les importations concernées et le dommage constaté. Cette conclusion repose sur l’analyse simultanée de l’évolution des volumes importés et des indicateurs de préjudice, ainsi que sur l’examen d’autres facteurs susceptibles d’avoir influencé la situation économique de l’industrie nationale. Au terme de son évaluation, le ministère conclut que l’augmentation des importations faisant l’objet de dumping a eu un effet défavorable sur la situation économique de la branche de production nationale et constitue l’une des principales causes du préjudice relevé. L’analyse des autres facteurs potentiels n’a, selon le rapport, révélé aucun élément présentant un impact négatif direct susceptible d’expliquer à lui seul la détérioration observée. Les autorités considèrent ainsi que les investigations menées ont permis de distinguer clairement les effets des différents facteurs connus de ceux imputables aux importations incriminées. Elles concluent donc, à ce stade de la procédure, à l’existence d’un lien de causalité établi entre les importations de panneaux de bois à âme épaisse originaires de Chine et d’Indonésie et le dommage subi par l’industrie nationale. L’avis DDC/11/2026 précise enfin que les parties intéressées peuvent consulter la version non confidentielle du rapport présentant les résultats préliminaires de l’enquête. Elles sont invitées à soumettre leurs observations, commentaires ou informations complémentaires, sous forme confidentielle et non confidentielle, dans le cadre de la poursuite de la procédure. items.description: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam’s commercial ⁠hub, is proposing ⁠to gradually restrict ⁠petrol- and diesel-powered vehicles from its downtown area from mid-2027, as part of a planned low-emission zone (LEZ), according to state-run Thanh Nien newspaper. items.title: Troops foil abduction attempt, rescue 14 victims in Zamfara
items.description: By Kingsley Omonobi Troops of Sector 2, Operation FANSAN YAMMA, have foiled an attempted abduction and rescued 14 kidnapped victims during an operation in Tsafe Local Government Area of Zamfara State. The operation, conducted on August 26, 2026, followed credible intelligence about suspicious activities around Magazu village. Acting on the information, the troops deployed to the area and encountered armed men allegedly attempting to abduct civilians, including motorists. The troops engaged the assailants, forcing them to abandon their vehicle and flee into nearby bushes. During a subsequent pursuit and search operation, the troops discovered and rescued 14 abducted victims. One of the rescued victims, who sustained gunshot wounds, was evacuated to the General Hospital, Tsafe, for medical treatment. No casualty was recorded among the troops during the operation. The successful operation, according to the military, underscores the continued efforts of Operation FANSAN YAMMA to protect civilians and deny criminal elements freedom of movement across Zamfara State. The post Troops foil abduction attempt, rescue 14 victims in Zamfara appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Pakistan's amateur radios are tuned in for the apocalypse
items.description: When the earthquake struck in 2005, two men in Islamabad loaded their bags and headed for Azad Kashmir. They made it as far as Kohala bridge where the road got cut off. From there on, they made it by foot and hitchhiked on motorcycles and the back of pick-up trucks to Muzaffarabad. One of the few offices still functioning there was Rescue 15 whose building had half collapsed. The men asked the surprised police officials inside if they had a car battery. The officials led them to a crushed Suzuki Mehran. The men got to work. A radio transceiver was plugged into the battery and they started transmitting messages to Islamabad since telephone landlines had collapsed. In the next few days they sent nearly 3,000 messages to Islamabad by radio, which their affiliates spread throughout Pakistan by phone. Most messages were confirmations of survivals and deaths. These men belonged to the voluntary Pakistan Amateur Radio Society (PARS) which has been around since 1970. It is made up of licensed professionals who operate amateur or ham radio, which keep people connected when all else fails. Decades later, the society is still going strong, and since its fledgling foray into Kashmir has increasingly taken up the cause of rescue and relief work when humanitarian disaster strikes in Pakistan. Ham radios come to Pakistan Ham radios emerged at the end of the 19th century with licensing starting from the US around 1912. One theory suggests that it was the initials of a group of early adopters—Hyman, Almy, and Murray at Harvard University’s radio club—that shortened first into HYALMU and then the name HAM. A more popular theory is that in the early days professionals looked down at the amateurs as ‘hams,’ as in ham-fisted or unskilled. Despite the pejorative etymology, the name stuck and is used proudly today. Amateur radio operators have operated here since before Partition. The oldest membership card was issued in November 1947 and a Pakistan Amateur Radio Society one from 1950 carries the call sign AP5B. Records show that one was active in Karachi in 1949 and from Quetta’s Chiltan Hotel in 1953. Old QSL cards from Pakistan (clockwise from top): From 1947 issued under the old VU call sign, from 1949 with the new Pakistani AP call sign, the oldest society card from 1950, and the card for Quetta’s Chiltan Hotel. Photos via PARS Though these records appear in 1950, former PARS President Nasir Khan (call sign AP2NK) said in a 2019 interview that the society was formed in 1970. (This discrepancy could be explained by a change in registration rules after which the society began anew). According to Nasir Khan, many of the initial members, including him, were associated with the telecommunications industry which is why their professional interests led them to ham radio, and ultimately to create the society. When Nasir Khan passed away in 2025, PARS announced that AP2NK was now a ‘silent key’. Ham radio work is driven by enthusiasm and charitable spirit but it is still governed by regulations which say a licensed operator has to be a member of PARS to legally function. Licenses were first issued by the Post and Telegraph department, followed by the Telephone and Telegraph department, and since 1996, the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) which now has a dedicated Radio-Based Services section. PTA records thus date back to 1962-63 even though files and folders have moved around between departments. Radio operators in Pakistan must be at least 16 years old. They join PARS as a ‘short-wave listener’ (SWL) for at least one year (like a driving learner’s license) before earning a full license (two years if you are under 18). SWLs can listen but not speak on the radio and use this time to learn mannerisms and techniques. Applications require details of equipment and operators are subjected to security verification which takes three months or more. A written test and interview follow at the PTA. Each newly licensed operator is then assigned a unique call sign, which in Pakistan begin with AP2 (or 5 for organisations) followed by the person’s initials. Radio communication takes place with phonetic codes, so AP2 will become “Alpha Papa 2”, and universally recognised Q codes, such as QTH relating to location and QSL relating to receipt of transmission. Codes such as “5 and 9”, meaning readability and signal strength respectively are at their highest, are also used. Audio of communication between hams in Islamabad and Lahore, a distance of over 283 kilometres. They announce their call signs, and confirm readability and signal strength by saying “5 and 9”. PARS helps applicants prepare and for several years, tests were conducted in coordination with the PTA. The license fee is Rs2,000 and has to be renewed every five years. Members pay the Society Rs2,000 a year, students Rs1,500 for three years and SWLs Rs4,000 for a three-year term. People over 65 years are granted lifetime licenses. Licenses can be revoked legally but according to the PTA no such case has arisen so far. Licenses usually end when holders pass away or fail to renew. The PTA does not allow mobile radio stations in its law. Exceptions can, however, be made for temporary periods in times of emergency and special need. This provision, in particular, is central to how the Society has worked in rescue efforts. ‘It’s not a hobby’ Today the group has around 600 active members of whom around 160 are amateur radio operators and the rest are SWLs or others. Most members have full-time jobs or businesses. One works in the oil and gas industry, some are telecom engineers, another is a cardiologist and several are serving members of the armed forces. Former Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Amir Gulistan Janjua (AP2AGJ) was also a member. There is nothing ‘amateur’ about PARS. During initial interviews, my use of the word ‘hobby’ was met with polite clarification that every member was a professional and the operations are considered a service. Indeed, the Facebook page and website lists PARS as a non-profit organization with coordinators and representatives in all provinces. It does not accept donations or raise funds and the rule is that no politics or personal matters can ever be discussed on air. Equipment is considered expensive but lasts decades. Members learn how to repair their own machines and one member even created a specialized battery that can power several radios at once. This spirit of invention also takes members to science fairs and expos. At an event in NUST in 2026, for example, PARS taught students how to make an antenna using a clothes hanger, with which they talked to someone in Gujranwala. Some of the society’s events, such as the annual meeting of its general body, take place at a university managed by one of the members. No premises have ever been acquired and the Society’s headquarters are generally based at the licensed location of a senior member. At one point it was a school owned by a senior office bearer and later another member’s house. The boy who loved radios I met the Society’s vice-president at his house in Islamabad that doubles as the organization’s headquarters. I had the location PIN and house number but when I got there, I realised I had wasted my time looking at plaques in the street. It was the house with the huge antenna. The antenna on the shack belonging to AP2AUM. Photo by author. In a ‘shack’ on the roof I met one of its oldest active members, Asadullah Marwat (call sign AP2AUM). He is in his fifties and has the congenial air of a man who has been around people a lot. When he speaks, he moves from anecdote to anecdote, a sign of a life full of experiences. He is a lawyer who worked his way up to Assistant Advocate General of the then NWFP before switching careers to the United Nations. Seasons have come and gone, Asadullah Marwat has changed cities for jobs and became a grandfather but the radio has been the one constant in his life. The set is switched on in his bedroom when he comes home from work, and it stays on until he falls asleep. For her latest birthday, Marwat gave his supportive wife a walkie-talkie, after finally finding one that fit in her purse as she had been demanding for years. Marwat’s first contact with radios came when he was a teenager living in Malakand, where his father was a government officer. His father had acquired walkie-talkies to coordinate poppy eradication in the district at a time when channels of communication were limited. With not much else to do, the young Asad got one and started fiddling around with it. He used makeshift antennas to increase the radio’s range until the antenna was so big that it started to bend over. The father and son were in the early days of their radio journeys when they learned about ham radios. A certain Farrukh Sahab (AP2FI) in Lahore had a powerful radio that he used to talk to “faraway places” so Marwat’s father loaded his children into the car and drove from Swat to Lahore to meet him. They watched in amazement when AP2FI talked to someone in Norway as a demonstration. A few years later the family went to the Industrial Expo in Islamabad, where they saw a stall set up by PARS. They also met the late Nasir Khan, the long-time president of PARS who explained how things worked. The inspired duo bought radios and were granted licenses a year later in 1993. Asadullah Marwat has been on air since then and served as vice-president since 2014-15. Asadullah Marwat (AP2AUM) in his shack. Photo by author Even with no disaster relief going on, he finds plenty of time to have fun. In 2019, he spoke to the International Space Station as it passed over Pakistan. Inside the shack, he fires up the High Frequency transceiver and rolls the knob until voices come into focus. “Russians,” he says with a laugh, as we both lean forward to listen. Connecting the hops PARS members often boast they are more adept than those who rely on radios for their professional duties. An instance that demonstrated this arose in 2021, when a PARS member was approached for help by policemen on duty in Azad Kashmir deputed at Chilehana, the southernmost entry point for district Neelum, making it a key check post. Their headquarters in Athmuqam was around 35km away by road. The policemen had been equipped with radios but they couldn’t contact the headquarters reliably unless one of them climbed to the top of a mountain with a clear line of sight. There was only one problem, Chilehana sits right next to the Line of Control, which meant that it wasn’t the greatest idea to have a man in uniform prowl around on a mountaintop looking for a signal. The task of solving this mystery fell to one of the Society’s experts, Mubeen Ajmal (AP2AJM) who had a degree in telecommunications engineering. As with many children from the 1980s and 1990s, Ajmal was a fan of the Urdu spy novels Imran Series in which radio communication was a recurring theme. He came across PARS at a seminar at the Federal Urdu University, where he studied in 2006. He remained an SWL for six years, until he graduated and was able to set up his own station and earned a license in 2012. Ajmal figured out that the radio transmission from the checkpost was failing to complete a ‘hop’ to the middle of the district, from where it would then hop again to reach the headquarters at Athmuqam. All it needed was some new hardware to get messages across. Antennas have a relation between dimensions and the frequencies they are best suited to. Ajmal asked for the exact frequencies the policemen operated on and fabricated a Yagi antenna (a popular directional antenna named after its Japanese founder) at his house with the precise measurements needed. He used the best material he could find, in this instance a green PVC pipe as a boom to prop up the antenna. Left: The antenna made by PARS on the Police check post with a green PVC pipe as boom. Right: The group that installed it, including Marwat (front) and Ajmal (red hat). Photos via Mubeen Ajmal After running computer-based and live simulations to see if his antenna was working, he then drove with Marwat and some other members to Neelum. They set up the antenna right outside the container checkpost. Within moments, the policeman’s handheld radio crackled. “Are you on the mountain again?” was the first thing the officer on the other end asked. “No sir, some men helped us fix the radio,” the man on duty replied. ‘Don’t let them leave.” The hams barely had a second to glance at each other, wondering if there was trouble, before the officer added that he wanted to invite them to dinner at his house. PARS has since signed an MoU with KP’s Rescue 1122 and helped restore or fix equipment in Galiyat and other regions. In August 2026, they travelled to Bahrain, in Swat, to fix an antenna that allowed the regional team to talk to headquarters again. When water kills power Inspired by the success in Kashmir, PARS started taking more interest in disaster relief. By the time the next one struck in 2010, the group was ready. One of the first casualties was electricity after the rivers swelled and enveloped swathes of Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Telecom towers soon ran out of power and communications went down. It would take months to get cellular networks back up. One PARS team working on connecting Nowshera and Charsadda to Islamabad and Peshawar. Another team linked Faisalabad, Multan and Sargodha to Lahore. PARS already had a 2-meter repeater but its coverage wasn’t extending to far-flung areas. To fix this, they installed cross-band repeaters so they could use handheld radios instead of being limited to base stations, which required electricity at a time when power was down. An aerial view of the floods in Dera Allah Yar in 2022. Photo via AFP Once members spread out, the relief work became easier. In a communique on August 20, 2010, PARS said that Pashtun Garhi and Pir Sabak in Nowshera needed tents, food and water for 15,000 displaced people. In Charsadda’s Mera Prang, they found 300 families without shelter. In Dharkhanawalla, Sargodha, they conveyed that entire villages were submerged. The group raised funds and collaborated with the Pakistan Academy of Family Physicians to bring in doctors and supplies, earning them a mention from the American Radio Relay League. When Sindh and Balochistan flooded in 2022 the team was able to venture further, reaching Badin, Thatta and Dera Allah Yar. Armed with the wisdom that it was better to remain mobile instead of setting up fixed base stations, this time they worked out of their vehicles. Marwat distributed handheld radios and the team spread out. A member would locate an emergency and call one of the doctor members. This way, the team managed to set up medical camps that helped almost 300 families. A call for help In August 2025, Buner’s Deputy Commissioner Kashif Qayyum found himself in a fix after his area was cut off by a catastrophic cloudburst. It took his team three days to restore road access but rescue operations had hit a snag. There was no way to decide where to send the excavators, tractors and ambulances at his disposal. The rain had decimated mobile networks and despite Qayyum’s calls for help, the PTA and telecom companies had been unable to restore signals. Assistant commissioners would head out to a distress spot, only to find that they had no way of conveying specifics to Qayyum or headquarters. Some of them were walking around for twenty minutes to find signals. What should have taken 30 minutes was taking three hours. Then, the DC remembered an old friend. Qayyum had been an SWL at one point and known Marwat since the early 2000s. One conversation and 48 hours later, PARS got three vehicles full of men and equipment to Buner. One of the men Marwat brought with him was Saqib Ashraf (AP2SAA), the society’s technical guru and equipment repair maestro because of his degree in electronics and communication engineering. (He fell in love with radio after seeing his first one in an uncle’s old army photos). Ashraf told me that Buner was one of the most challenging sites, because they wanted to get communications up in a single night. A base station in the DC’s office was their best shot at securing line-of-sight access. The men pointed the antenna in the direction of Pir Baba which was worst affected. A repeater was set up in Police Lines and official vehicles were equipped with radios. Key officials heading into the field were given handheld radios set to the PARS frequency. Left to right: PARS at work, the finished antenna, the devastation in Buner. Photos via PARS Suddenly, everything eased. Even in numerous ‘bowls’ between the Buner mountains, the radios did not lose coverage. Ambulances and excavators were dispatched as soon as a need was identified, to even the remotest parts of the district. The set-up was so successful that it runs to this day. Qayyum is now posted to Peshawar from where he told me that the experience showed him the impact of ham radios on district management. He argues that they could revolutionize forest range patrols and even security operations during Muharram, when phone signals are restricted. What’s next for PARS? A December 2002 issue of Australian Amateur Radio Magazine featured PARS which had around 170 active radio operators in 2000. The number is roughly the same 26 years later. At least 1,200 members are needed for ample coverage across the country. By comparison, India has over 44,000 operators and the US above 800,000. The earthquake-prone Japan had 1.2 million operators at one point even though its population and area are half of Pakistan’s. It isn’t expensive to take up amateur radio. A $25 portable unit will connect you to the same frequencies as the big setups. The PTA fees are among the lowest in the world (Rs2,000 for five-year licenses, Rs100 for tests) even though they barely cover the cost of the license document it issues. Applications and testing cost $50 in the US (Rs13,000) and at least ¥4,300 in Japan (Rs7,500). It is, however, a process to acquire a license in Pakistan, which is perhaps the only one in the world needing law-enforcement clearance. It can take longer than the stipulated 12 weeks and rejections are not always clearly explained. It takes less than a week for testing and licensing in the US and UK, and a month in Japan. India also conducts security clearances, but after its test. Of course, not everyone knows about ham radios in an age of smartphones, which might explain the low numbers. But as the last twenty years have shown this generation, networks do go down in urban and rural disasters, making ham radio a more important back-up than ever. Saqib Ashraf (AP2SAA) and others will warn you that ham radio isn’t a hobby or for cute drawing room show-and-tell. You have to respond in emergencies, pick up and travel to remote areas on your own steam, to make sure someone in distress can get a short message out. Back at the shack, Marwat switches on the transceiver to check if anyone else is on air. There is a crackle and the message comes out: “Flood warnings are coming in, I think we should start preparing.” Header image by Mohsin Alam, based on photos from PARS

items.title: Tunisie | Du souverainisme à la question numide, ou l’opposition aveugle
items.description: Les récents articles** publiés dans Kapitalis font table rase du passé d’une manière somme toute radicale. De surcroît, l’idéologie souverainiste à la base de sa réflexion est assez insolite dans un pays par nature tolérant dont les élites se vantent volontiers d’être cosmopolites. Dr Mounir Hanablia * Je dis bien souverainiste, le nationalisme au Maghreb étant d'essence arabo- musulmane, comme si dans le contexte le sentiment de tunisianité était exclusif, opposable à toute autre appartenance. C’est déjà faire insulte à la double nationalité. L’auteur des articles ne laisse donc d’autre choix que de remonter le cours de l’Histoire afin de relativiser le bien-fondé de ses thèses. On veut bien admettre l’existence d'un souverainisme tunisien dont il serait le fondateur, sans la référence à la bataille de Legnano. Mais dans ce cas pourquoi le limiter à la borne 233 ou aux redevances gazières ? Il n’est venu à l’esprit de quiconque de réclamer la souveraineté sur la Sicile qui pendant deux siècles a fait partie de l’émirat aghlabide de Kairouan, Fatimide de Mahdia ou Ziride, ou bien sur le Mezzogiorno quand Bari était le chef-lieu d’un émirat. Mais revenons à l’époque moderne et à l’indépendance de la Tunisie. Force est d’admettre dans la polémique engendrée par ses opinions que l’impulsion décisive en faveur de l’indépendance au Maghreb est bien constituée par le débarquement américain au Maroc qui aboutira à la défaite des Nazis en Tunisie en juin 1943, ainsi que la volonté clairement exprimée par le président Roosevelt et ses représentants, ou bien perçue comme telle par les leaders nationalistes, de liquider l’empire français. La suite est donc dans l’ordre normal des choses même si l’affrontement Est-Ouest la retarde inévitablement. Le Vietnam en 1954, le Maroc et la Tunisie en 1956, obtiennent l’indépendance. Seule l’Algérie du fait de son statut de territoire français pose problème, l’armée de Challe et de Salan qui émerge de l’humiliation de Dien Bien Phu avec une terrible soif de revanche refuse de l’abandonner et envisage la constitution d’une Algérie européenne sécessionniste, un Israël français. L’Algérie est bien une création de la France Cependant en 1962, elle accède à l’indépendance dans le cadre des accords d’Evian et le Sahara lui est attribué. Ainsi ce pays, contrairement à ses voisins, ne disposait d’aucun Etat unitaire en 1830. C’est bien une création de la France dont la colonne vertébrale est constituée non par la bourgeoisie citadine comme en Tunisie, ni par le Palais comme au Maroc, mais par les ultimes détenteurs de la force seule à même de maintenir la cohésion de cet immense espace, les prétoriens. A ce titre l’État algérien est bien le successeur en droite ligne de l’État colonial français forgé par les troupes de Bugeaud et du Duc d’Aumale. Malgré un vernis de socialisme, la coopération entre la métropole et l’ex- colonie, pas plus qu’avec les Américains, ne se démentira jamais, en particulier au Sahara dans le domaine des essais nucléaires ainsi que les exploitations du gaz et des hydrocarbures. Contrairement à ce que d’aucuns affirment actuellement, c’est sciemment que la frontière algéro-tunisienne a été délimitée par la puissance coloniale et dans son intérêt. Et le Président Bourguiba l’a bien compris. Il n’était en effet pas question d’assurer au pays contrôlant Bizerte et le détroit de Sicile la part d’hydrocarbures et de gaz qui lui eût assuré la puissance. Tunisie – Algérie | Le grand reniement de l’été 1962 Bourguiba et la question des frontières Bourguiba toujours visionnaire admettra également en réglant la question de la frontière ne pas vouloir chez lui d’un problème numide, c’est-à-dire d’un irrédentisme des habitants des montagnes de l’Ouest qui acceptent mal le diktat de populations côtières se prévalant de l’unité nationale et qui brandissent le drapeau du pays voisin dans des manifestations de protestation contre une politique de développement inégalitaire. C’est d’ailleurs du bassin minier à l’Ouest que naîtra l’incendie qui jettera à bas le régime de Ben Ali. Cependant l’Algérie elle-même en butte à un irrédentisme kabyle soutenu par Israël peut difficilement tabler sur la partition de la Tunisie ; il lui en coûterait la sécession de toute sa partie orientale pour former une nouvelle Numidie forcément hostile. Néanmoins des arguments souverainistes totalement étrangers à la nature de notre pays prennent pour cible le voisin de l’Ouest, jugé hégémoniste. L’Etat, le nôtre, est accusé de complaisance coupable dans ses rapports avec lui, notamment sur la question du gaz. L’Histoire est là pour rappeler que Carthage fut une colonie étrangère, que Massinissa le Roi des Numides a bien contribué à sa destruction, que l’Afrique du Nord a été dans son ensemble une province romaine, arabe, française, que l’armée française est arrivée en Tunisie en 1881 en provenance d’Algérie pour imposer le protectorat, et que les enfants de Hussein Ben Ali Turki n’ont dû qu’au Dey d’Alger d’être rétablis sur le trône de leur père. A l’inverse, c’est bien sûr à nos frontières que l’ALN algérienne s’est constituée en vue de prendre le pouvoir, avec le total assentiment de la puissance coloniale sur le départ. Aujourd’hui et de nouveau on tient rigueur à Bourguiba de l’avoir accepté pour fustiger l’ingratitude. Mais que vaut la gratitude en politique ? C’est tout juste si on ne précise pas qu’on eût dû aider le colonel Tahar Zbiri en fuite chez nous à prendre le pouvoir à Alger, ou bien que de là-bas Ahmed Ben Salah ou Nabil Karoui, pour ne pas dire Mohamed Mzali, eussent dû trouver l’aide fraternelle nécessaire à la chute de la tyrannie. Qu’à cela ne tienne ; c’est désormais dans le Hirak, pour ne pas dire le MAK, que nous devons selon nos souverainistes placer nos espoirs d’entretenir des relations apaisées et équilibrées. Mais les acteurs politiques peuvent se suivre sans se ressembler, les réalités géostratégiques elles sont immuables, ainsi que le prouve du Chah aux mollahs la volonté iranienne de maîtriser le nucléaire. Peut-on remettre en question l’intégrité territoriale de son pays ? Avant donc de parler de jugulaire, de goulot de bouteille, ou d’étranglement, ou de terrorisme importé avec un parti Ennahdha au pouvoir, il convient de savoir s’il est dans l’intérêt de la Tunisie d’avoir à ses portes un nouvel Etat numide soutenu de l’étranger doté d’une idéologie expansionniste et revancharde qui rogne sur son territoire et pour qui Carthage ne soit qu’un ramassis d’envahisseurs. Si donc le pouvoir tunisien est déstabilisé par les grèves, les pannes, les pénuries, ou selon certains, l’incompétence, et que l’opposition pour parvenir à ses fins est capable de placer son destin entre les mains de ceux qui remettent en question l’intégrité territoriale de son propre pays, faut-il s’étonner que nos voisins envisagent des projets alternatifs exclusifs à l'écoulement du gaz ? Dans le contexte conflictuel que nous connaissons qui frappe la mer Rouge et le Golfe Persique, arguer des difficultés techniques de l’entreprise pour en faire un simple outil de propagande ne tient compte ni de la volonté européenne de garantir son approvisionnement énergétique, ni de le sécuriser, ni de l’évolution constante des moyens techniques disponibles vers plus d’efficacité. C’est dire combien minutieusement l’opposition doit choisir le panier où placer ses œufs. * Médecin de libre pratique. ** L’auteur fait allusion aux articles de l’ambassadeur Elyes Kasri sur le Transmed et la nécessité pour la Tunisie de mieux défendre ses intérêts dans le passage par ses territoires de ce gazoduc transportant le gaz algérien vers l’Italie. La Tunisie, goulot énergétique de l’Europe et jugulaire de l’Algérie L’article Tunisie | Du souverainisme à la question numide, ou l’opposition aveugle est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: US hails Dangote Refinery as Nigeria’s petroleum exports surge sevenfold
items.description: By Udeme Akpan, Energy Editor The Dangote Petroleum Refinery has been identified as the key driver behind a seven-fold increase in Nigeria’s seaborne petroleum product exports since 2023, according to the latest report by the United States Energy Information Administration (EIA). The U.S. agency disclosed that Nigeria’s seaborne petroleum product shipments averaged 561,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the second quarter of 2026, a significant increase from the annual average of 79,000 bpd recorded in 2023. According to the EIA, the growth in exports has strengthened Nigeria’s position in the international petroleum products market at a time when supplies from several other regions have faced constraints. The agency noted that the increase was largely underpinned by the commencement of operations at the Dangote Petroleum Refinery in January 2024. Data from energy intelligAence firm Vortexa showed that of the 561,000-bpd shipped during the second quarter of 2026, about 350,000 bpd were exported, compared to an annual average of 46,000 bpd in 2023. The EIA stated that increased production from the refinery has transformed Nigeria’s petroleum products market by reducing dependence on imports and boosting domestic supply. “With increased supply of petroleum products from the country’s largest refinery, imports fell, exports increased, and Nigeria became more self-sufficient in refined petroleum products,” the agency said. Before the start-up of the Dangote Refinery, Nigeria’s state-owned refineries collectively shipped less than 100,000 bpd of petroleum products, both domestically and internationally. The EIA observed that shipments rose significantly following the refinery’s commencement of operations and received a further boost after maintenance and expansion activities were completed in February 2026. The agency explained that the refinery’s crude distillation capacity increased from 650,000 bpd to 700,000 bpd following the completion of the expansion programme, enabling higher output and greater product availability. According to the report, total petroleum product shipments increased further as supply disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz created additional demand for alternative sources of refined products. The EIA reported that intra-Nigerian shipments reached 211,000 bpd in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 81,000 bpd in 2025 and 33,000 bpd in 2023, reflecting the refinery’s growing role in supplying fuel across the country. The post US hails Dangote Refinery as Nigeria’s petroleum exports surge sevenfold appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Crude imports by domestic refineries jump 151.5% in July — NMDPRA
items.description: By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja Crude oil imports by domestic refineries rose by 151.5 per cent to 5.13 million barrels in July 2026, from 2.04 million barrels in June, according to data released by the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA). The increase came as domestic crude supply to refineries fell sharply during the month. The NMDPRA’s July 2026 Midstream and Downstream Statistics showed that refineries received a total of 17.88 million barrels of crude in July, comprising 12.75 million barrels supplied domestically and 5.13 million barrels imported. Imported crude therefore accounted for 28.7 per cent of total crude receipts by domestic refineries in July, while domestic supplies contributed the remaining 71.3 per cent. The 5.13 million barrels imported in July represented a significant rebound from the 2.04 million barrels recorded in June. It was also higher than the 2.08 million barrels imported in May and 0.41 million barrels in April. However, July’s import volume remained below the 9.43 million barrels recorded in March, the highest monthly volume so far in 2026. The data showed that crude imports stood at 0.71 million barrels in January before rising to 4.25 million barrels in February and peaking at 9.43 million barrels in March. Imports subsequently plunged to 0.41 million barrels in April, before recovering to 2.08 million barrels in May, 2.04 million barrels in June and 5.13 million barrels in July. The report also disclosed that domestic crude supply to refineries declined by 25.4 per cent month-on-month, falling from 17.08 million barrels in June to 12.75 million barrels in July. In January, domestic refineries received 8.83 million barrels of domestic crude and 0.71 million barrels of imported crude, bringing total receipts to 9.54 million barrels. The figure rose to 13.13 million barrels in February, comprising 8.88 million barrels of domestic crude and 4.25 million barrels of imports. March recorded the highest total crude receipts at 20.92 million barrels, with domestic supply contributing 11.49 million barrels and imports 9.43 million barrels. Total receipts stood at 18.37 million barrels in April, made up of 17.96 million barrels of domestic crude and 0.41 million barrels of imports. In May, refineries received 17.92 million barrels, comprising 15.84 million barrels of domestic crude and 2.08 million barrels of imports, while June recorded 19.12 million barrels, made up of 17.08 million barrels of domestic crude and 2.04 million barrels of imports. Dangote refinery performance The NMDPRA data also showed that the Dangote Refinery operated at an average capacity utilisation of 71.09 per cent in July. The refinery produced an average of 25.9 million litres of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS), 19.1 million litres of Automotive Gas Oil (AGO) and 15.6 million litres of Aviation Turbine Kerosene (ATK) per day. Its average domestic receipts stood at 25.8 million litres per day for PMS, 15.7 million litres for AGO and 1.9 million litres for ATK. The refinery also exported 3.4 million litres of PMS, 11 million litres of AGO and 11.6 million litres of ATK per day as of July 31. Its closing stock at the end of July stood at 446.1 million litres of PMS, 162.3 million litres of AGO and 217.4 million litres of ATK. items.title: Women becoming part of Ghana’s political architecture – Joyce Bawah Mogtari
items.description: Senior Presidential Advisor and Senior Aide to President John Dramani Mahama, Joyce Bawah Mogtari, says women are increasingly becoming an integral part of Ghana’s political architecture, occupying influential roles beyond traditional positions as candidates, communicators and supporters. Reflecting on her political journey in a Facebook post, Madam Bawah Mogtari said her appointment by then-President John Dramani Mahama to succeed Hannah Tetteh came at a time when some questioned whether she was sufficiently experienced. She said the NDC’s subsequent defeat in the election presented her with the opportunity to grow, eventually becoming one of the regular voices speaking for the former President and the party. She also highlighted what she described as President Mahama’s deliberate effort to create space for women in political leadership, pointing to his choice of Professor Naana Jane Opoku-Agyemang as his running mate in two successive electoral cycles. She said the NDC’s return to power in 2024 has since seen women occupy positions as ministers, deputy ministers, chief executives, deputy chief executives and Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives. “I see women becoming part of the political architecture not merely as candidates, communicators or supporters, but as trusted advisers, strategists, aides and decision-makers operating at the highest levels of political leadership,” she said. Madam Bawah Mogtari acknowledged that women continue to face challenges relating to parity, visibility and recognition, but said the growing number of women in political leadership signals progress, adding that “the most powerful form of political communication is not simply talking about women’s representation. It is making women’s representation normal.”

items.title: Mayor Mamdani opposes NYC event with leader of India's Hindu nationalist group
items.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Tuesday he did not support an upcoming event in his city featuring the leader of the Hindu nationalist group that is the ideological parent of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), is scheduled to speak at a Manhattan event on Saturday, according to the event’s website. “I don’t support the rally, but I don’t know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,” Mamdani, who is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor of New York City, said when asked if the event should be cancelled. “The vision of India that I was taught by my family and one that I grew up being very familiar with was of a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India. And it has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision.” The event’s website casts the August 29 gathering as the “Universal Oneness Celebration” bringing together the Hindu American community. The organisers, American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, say the event is backed by several Hindu American groups and promotes shared heritage and interfaith unity. Many local organisations have criticised it over Bhagwat’s attendance and the RSS’ history. The RSS, a powerful Hindu group from which Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s BJP emerged, said in May it had organised foreign visits, including to the US, to counter perceptions it is a paramilitary outfit involved in attacks on minority communities. The US Commission on International Religious Freedom says the RSS “has been involved in acts of extreme violence and intolerance against members of minority groups for decades”. The RSS disputes intolerance accusations and says it is a “Hindu-centric civilisational, cultural movement” whose goal is to “carry the nation to the pinnacle of glory”, including by uniting Hindus. United Nations and human rights groups say abuse of Indian minorities has risen in recent years, pointing to rising hate speeches , a religion-based citizenship law , the demolition of Muslim-owned properties, the removal of occupied Kashmir’s autonomy and an anti-conversion legislation that challenges freedom of belief. The BJP-led Indian government denies being discriminatory and says its policies, including food subsidy programmes and electrification drives, benefit all communities.

items.title: Fidelity Bank completes renovation of multipurpose auditorium at Police Public Safety Training School
items.description: Fidelity Bank Ghana has completed a full renovation of the Multipurpose Auditorium at the Police Public Safety Training School (PPSTS) in Pwalugu, reaffirming a partnership with the Ghana Police Service that now spans a decade of sustained support. The newly refurbished facility provides an improved space for training, conferences, strategic engagements, and other institutional activities. The Multipurpose Auditorium was officially handed over at a ceremony where Harold Ansah, Head of Personal Banking at Fidelity Bank, represented the bank and presented it to the Director of PPSTS, Assistant Commissioner of Police, Dr Wilson Aniagyei. The renovation marks the latest chapter in a relationship in which Fidelity Bank has consistently invested in the institution’s training infrastructure and welfare over the past ten years. That history of support has taken several forms. Over the years, Fidelity Bank has contributed to the school’s training and safety needs by constructing a mechanised borehole, upgrading the kitchen facilities, and providing essential equipment such as cookers, gas cylinders, dining tables, and benches to support the institution’s daily operations. The renovation of the Multipurpose Auditorium — a facility that had fallen into disrepair, its condition worsened by years of rain damage — represents the most extensive intervention to date, restoring a critical space to full functionality. Speaking on behalf of Godfred Attafuah, Divisional Director of Retail Banking, Harold Ansah said the investment reflected the bank’s broader understanding of its role in national life. “The men and women who pass through this institution dedicate their lives to protecting the rest of us, and the least we can do is ensure they have proper spaces in which to learn, train, and prepare for that responsibility,” he said. “By investing in the spaces where our law enforcement professionals learn and strategise, we are reinforcing our commitment to national security and community well-being. This is not a transaction. It is a partnership we intend to sustain.” Mr Ansa further expressed the Bank’s appreciation to the Ghana Police Service for the partnership over the years, noting that Fidelity Bank remains committed to identifying opportunities where its resources and expertise can contribute to institutional development. Receiving the facility, ACP Dr Aniagyei expressed deep appreciation to Fidelity Bank on behalf of the Inspector General of Police, commending the bank for its consistency and for standing with the service over so many years. The latest intervention comes at a time when the development of a well-trained, professional and adequately supported police service remains critical to maintaining public safety and strengthening confidence in Ghana’s security institutions. He noted that the renovated auditorium would directly benefit successive cohorts of recruits and expressed the institution’s desire to see the relationship with Fidelity Bank continue and deepen in the years ahead. For Fidelity Bank, the renovation is consistent with a long-held conviction that its responsibilities extend beyond banking into the institutions and communities that hold the nation together. In restoring a space where those charged with public safety are trained, the bank sees an investment not only in a building, but in the people and the mission it serves

items.title: 'A privilege, not a right': US to revoke visas of up to 200,000 asylum seekers
items.description: The US government plans to revoke the visas of foreigners who came to the country for tourism or business but sought to stay longer by applying for asylum, the State Department said on Tuesday. The crackdown marks another step in the Trump administration’s signature drive to reduce immigration into the United States. The administration said it is now working with the Department of Homeland Security to identify and revoke the visas of people who, it said, came to America billing themselves as temporary visitors but then applied for asylum so they could stay permanently. “Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud — which is grounds for visa revocation,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement that confirmed press reports about the new policy. The White House, in a post on X, suggested “up to two hundred thousand visas” would be affected and claimed it would be the “largest mass visa revocation in history”. The State Department neither confirmed nor denied that number. Pigott said, “The number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis.” Early this month, the department said that since President Donald Trump returned to power in January 2025, some 175,000 foreigners had seen their US visas revoked on grounds ranging from criminal offenses, including driving under the influence, to praising the killing of the right-wing activist Charlie Kirk. The administration also recently revoked the visas of Mexican officials, including the son of the former president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador. This prompted a complaint from the current president, Claudia Sheinbaum. Trump, who won reelection in large part on his promise to fight illegal immigration, has expelled huge numbers of people who were in the country without proper residence papers. But he has also worked to restrict the entry of foreigners who do go by the rules and has gone after those who overstay their visas after they expire. Some of these measures have been challenged and curtailed by the courts. Last Friday a federal judge struck down a government ban on visas to nationals from 75 countries who wish to settle in the country indefinitely. These countries included Afghanistan, Brazil, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Nigeria, Somalia, Thailand and Yemen. The Trump administration is also planning to expand vetting of the social media accounts of visa applicants. “We are making clear that a visa is a privilege — not a right,” Pigott said on Tuesday.

items.title: Oil prices slide 2% on Iran-Oman talks to reopen Strait of Hormuz
items.description: Oil prices dropped about 2% on Wednesday, adding to the previous session’s losses, on fresh hopes ‌the Strait of Hormuz could reopen after Iran said it had resumed talks with neighbour Oman on managing the strategic waterway. Brent crude futures fell $1.78, or 2.0%, to $86.80 a barrel by 0027 GMT, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $1.49, ​or 1.8%, at $80.87. Both benchmarks lost more than 3% on Tuesday. “The market continues to react to ​developments surrounding navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, and hopes for progress in talks ⁠between Iran and Oman have triggered selling,” said Mitsuru Muraishi, an analyst at Fujitomi Securities. “That said, uncertainty ​over the outlook has prompted bargain buying, limiting further losses, and prices are likely to remain range-bound for the ​time being,” he added. Iran said it had restarted talks with Oman to manage the Strait as it faces heightened economic pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump. Iran and Oman have been in on-and-off talks for weeks about controlling traffic through the waterway, which ​handled one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war began in February. The two countries ​said on Tuesday that they discussed “a joint temporary navigational corridor” through the strait and agreed to clear it of mines. Despite ‌the ongoing ⁠tensions, the U.S. is beginning to send personnel back to some diplomatic missions in the Middle East that were evacuated or downsized amid tensions with Iran, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters. The move suggests Washington sees a lower risk of the conflict with Iran escalating in the near term, though some embassies will ​initially operate below full capacity. On ​Monday, Washington expanded sanctions aimed ⁠at cutting off Iran’s economic lifeline, threatening to punish countries that continue to do business with Tehran, though it said it would not impose penalties immediately. Separately, an ​oil tanker was struck on Tuesday by an unidentified projectile and disabled about 9 ​nautical miles (17 km) ⁠northeast of Oman’s Ash Shishah, which lies at the entrance to the strait, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said. In the U.S., the American Petroleum Institute reported that crude oil inventories rose by about 4.2 million barrels in the week ended August 21, market sources said. Analysts polled by Reuters estimated crude oil stockpiles ​would rise by about 600,000 barrels on average. Official data from the EIA, the statistical arm of the U.S. Department of Energy, ​are due at 10:30 a.m. ET (1430 GMT) on Wednesday.

items.title: Stakeholders trained in parametric insurance and disaster risk financing
items.description: Scores of stakeholders from government institutions have undergone training in parametric insurance and disaster risk financing as part of efforts to strengthen Ghana’s preparedness for climate-related disasters, particularly flooding. The four-day capacity development programme, organised by the National Disaster Management Organisation (NADMO) and the Ministry of Finance in collaboration with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), is being held from August 24 to 27, 2026, at the Capital View Hotel in the Eastern Region. The training, dubbed “UNDP Ghana Capacity Development Training on Disaster Risk Financing, Flood Risk Modelling, Technical Assistance Deployment and Payout Management,” brought together representatives from Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs), NADMO, the National Insurance Commission (NIC), Ghana Statistical Service (GSS), National Development Planning Commission (NDPC), Ghana Hydrological Authority and Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs) within the Greater Accra Metropolitan Area. The programme is designed to strengthen institutional knowledge and practical capacity in disaster risk financing, flood risk modelling and the management of financial protection mechanisms. On the second day of the programme, consultant Dr Yazidu Ustarz took participants through the principles of parametric insurance, including how predefined triggers determine insurance payouts. He explained that parametric insurance differs from conventional insurance because payouts are based on the occurrence of a measurable event reaching an agreed threshold rather than an assessment of the actual damage suffered. Using flooding as an example, Dr Ustarz said a parametric flood insurance policy for an institution such as NADMO could specify a particular rainfall or river-level threshold. Once the agreed threshold is reached, based on data from an approved weather station, satellite or other agreed measurement system, the insurer can make the predetermined payment without necessarily sending an adjuster to assess the physical damage. He said the central question in parametric insurance was whether the agreed event had reached the predetermined trigger. According to him, parametric insurance can be designed to cover a range of risks, including floods, droughts, hurricanes and strong winds, agricultural losses, earthquakes and travel or aviation disruptions. For instance, drought insurance could trigger a payout when rainfall falls below a specified level, while flood insurance could make a payment when rainfall or river levels exceed an agreed threshold. Dr Ustarz said one of the major advantages of parametric insurance was the potential for faster payouts because the payment mechanism was linked to independently verifiable data rather than a lengthy claims assessment. He, however, cautioned participants about false basis risk, which occurs when the insurance trigger does not perfectly correspond with the actual loss experienced. He explained that a policyholder could suffer significant damage without the agreed trigger being reached, resulting in no payout. Conversely, a trigger could be reached even when the actual impact of the event was relatively small which can be called false positive basis risk. He therefore stressed the importance of selecting appropriate triggers, measurement systems and thresholds when designing parametric insurance products. The National Coordinator of the Insurance and Risk Finance Facility (IRFF) at UNDP Ghana, Dr Amina Sammo, described disaster risk financing as more than a financial instrument, saying it was an important component of sustainable development. She said millions of people remained vulnerable to the effects of disasters and that a single flood, failed harvest or other economic shock could wipe out years of progress made by families and communities. Dr Sammo said resilience depended on strong institutions, effective policies, reliable data, early warning systems and financial mechanisms that enabled individuals, businesses and governments to recover more quickly after disasters. She identified disaster risk financing as a critical tool for protecting livelihoods, supporting small businesses, encouraging farmers to invest with greater confidence and helping governments manage the fiscal risks associated with disasters. According to her, the UNDP, through its Insurance and Risk Finance Facility, continues to work with countries around the world to strengthen financial resilience through innovative insurance and risk financing solutions. The training is expected to equip participating institutions with practical knowledge to improve Ghana’s ability to anticipate, finance and respond to the financial consequences of climate-related disasters, particularly flooding.

items.title: Telecoms operator MTN eyes banking licences as it pushes deeper into lending
items.description: Africa’s largest telecoms operator, MTN Group, is exploring banking licences in select markets as the company looks to expand lending ​from its own balance sheet, CEO Ralph Mupita said on Tuesday. MTN ‌is stepping up its push into fintech services to drive growth beyond traditional telecommunications revenue, with lending emerging as one of the fastest-growing segments within its mobile money business. “We’re ​seeing good growth on advanced services, which are our future-proof services,” ​Mupita told journalists, referring to offerings such as payments, e-commerce and ⁠lending. “The big growth now, which will be the growth of the future, ​is actually lending.” MTN currently provides loans through partnerships with banks. “We’re beginning to explore, ​where it makes sense and where there are large customer bases (and) significant floats in wallets, whether it may make sense to have some sort of banking licence that enables ​us to take deposits,” Mupita said. “As such, we will then be lending ​over time off our own balance sheet. But also, it doesn’t mean we won’t do ‌any ⁠partnership lending.” He said the approach would be selective rather than implemented across all of MTN’s operations, and that any move to balance-sheet lending would be gradual given the risks involved. DATA CENTRES MTN is also betting on digital infrastructure growth. The ​company plans to develop ​AI-enabled data centres ⁠in South Africa and Nigeria through Africa Data Hub Holding, a venture with an undisclosed UAE-backed investor to develop ​AI-ready data centre infrastructure across key African markets. Mupita said ​MTN would ⁠be a minority investor in the venture, while its partner, which has experience building data centres in the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf countries, would provide ⁠most ​of the capital and technical expertise. The initial phase is expected to target about 150 megawatts of capacity across South Africa and Nigeria, with future ​expansion driven by demand, he added.
