items.title: Partisan solidarity overrides accountability – Dr Dramani accuses Parliament of protecting its own
items.description: Executive Director of the Africa Centre for Parliamentary Affairs, Dr Rasheed Dramani, has accused Parliament of repeatedly failing to hold its own members accountable when serious allegations are made against them. He said partisan loyalty often takes precedence over the scrutiny expected from lawmakers, contributing to growing public perceptions that Parliament is corrupt. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, Dr Dramani said his concern goes beyond the allegations involving Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin. He said the controversy should instead force Parliament to examine the credibility of the office and the institution itself. “And for me, when this issue broke out, I was very worried not about Afenyo-Markin, but, as Inusah Fuseini said, about that office, particularly at a time when we have a supermajority parliament.” According to Dr Dramani, Ghana needs parliamentary leaders with sufficient integrity to hold the Executive accountable, particularly under a supermajority. “We need leaders with integrity. We need a minority with a very high level of integrity to be able to hold this supermajority and the executive accountable.” He said his concerns deepened after reflecting on persistent low levels of public trust in Parliament and high perceptions of corruption. Dr Dramani said one major factor is MPs’ tendency to rally around colleagues facing allegations without first demanding answers. “I think the first one is that over the years we have seen in our parliament that partisan solidarity overrides accountability.” “So you accuse one person, then an entire caucus begins to rally around that person without even asking the critical question.” He said the public’s perception of Parliament is further worsened when lawmakers accused of wrongdoing appear before court and receive broad support from colleagues. “We saw over the years MPs accused, and they are in court. Any time they are going to court, the whole parliament is empty. It increases that level of perception of mistrust.” Dr Dramani also questioned whether Parliament applies the same scrutiny to itself that it applies to the Executive. “Parliament is better at scrutinising the executive than having the moral authority to scrutinise itself,” he said. He cited the work of the Public Accounts Committee as an example, noting that it held about 31 public hearings in 2024 and made more than 1,000 recommendations for recovery of resources. “Does it apply the same kind of standard to its own whenever we hear some of these issues?” He also blamed the political cost of investigating fellow MPs for the reluctance to pursue such allegations. “The political cost of, you know, investigating themselves, their own, is usually very high, and they would rather keep quiet because, over the years, they build relationships; current MPs are future ministers, and all kinds of networks and so on.” The comments come amid the dispute between Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin and GoldBod Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi. Mr Gyamfi accused Mr Afenyo-Markin of extortion during a public dispute over criticism of GoldBod. Mr Afenyo-Markin rejected the allegation and threatened legal action, leading to a wider suing brouhaha. The Minority Leader has since gone to court, while the Office of the Special Prosecutor is conducting a preliminary assessment to determine whether to open a full investigation. Dr Dramani said the current controversy presents Parliament with an opportunity to demonstrate that allegations against its members can be resolved transparently. “What Parliament hasn’t done for itself over the years is that we haven’t seen a clear path from allegation to resolution.” He said Parliament should consider involving independent figures in any investigation. “I am hoping, Evans, that maybe for the first time we would have a committee that is made up not only of MPs.” He proposed a committee comprising MPs and eminent Ghanaians if Parliament does not opt for an external investigative body. “Maybe a committee of parliament that is made up of MPs and some eminent Ghanaians, so that for the first time, and in the interest of Parliament itself, in order to improve its image in the eyes of the public, that this matter is dealt with.” Dr Dramani said the outcome must be clear, whether the allegations are proven or dismissed. “Let us see a clear path from this allegation to a clear resolution, and if there are sanctions, let them be applied; if there are exonerations, let those happen.”

items.title: Deaths in Township police custody: Forensic report confirms women were addicts: IGP
items.description: LAHORE: Punjab Inspector General of Police (IGP) Abdul Kareem says the forensic report of the two young women, who had died in Township police station, has confirmed that they had been using addictive drugs or prohibited substances. Addressing a press conference here on Tuesday, along with other senior officers of Lahore police, he said the forensic report was prepared by a medical board comprising senior doctors. The IGP said that according to the report, both young women died of cardiopulmonary arrest, an acute medical emergency where the heart suddenly stops pumping blood and breathing ceases. He said the report also revealed that the women were using nine kinds of intoxicating substances which led to their death during interrogation in the police custody. To a question, the IGP said that though death of the two women at the same time was unusual, the forensic reports have made it clear that they died of addictive substance. About the progress in the investigation into Hina Javed’s murder case registered in Rawalpindi, the IGP said that three suspects were nominated in the FIR and two of them have been arrested by the police. The victim was found dead in the washroom of her apartment in a housing scheme in Rawalpindi on Thursday evening. The police said the body bore signs of torture, with a wire around the neck and it was tied to the shower rod. The IGP said the Rawalpindi police handled the case professionally by proving during investigations that it was a murder, not a suicide case. The investigations into the Hina Javed’s murder case are underway and the police will soon bring the culprits to the court of law, he added. Talking about the murder of Abdullah Tahir, a PTI ticket-holder from Okara, he said the shooters who targeted the victim fled to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Punjab police teams are working on the case to trace and arrest them as soon as possible. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Israeli MP smashes West Bank memorial under army escort
items.description: • Tel Aviv begins evicting UN training centre for Palestinians • West Bank settlers attack journalists, activists near Bethlehem RAMALLAH: A far-right Israeli lawmaker took a sledgehammer to a Palestinian memorial in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday while under military escort. Footage circulating on­­line showed Zvi Sukkot, who is also a settler and activist, smashing a monument commemorating “martyrs” in the Pales­ti­nian village of Madama in the northern West Bank, while soldiers stood nearby. “A few days ago, I demanded that the military take action to remove the monuments commemorating ter­­rorists in the murderers’ villages of Madama and Burin. Unfortu­na­tely, they remained in place. So, I went there myself and took action to re­­m­ove them,” Sukkot posted on Face­book, along with a video of the act. The Israeli military said Sukkot and his aides had conducted a “tour” of the area “with security provided by IDF soldiers who had been diverted from their operational activities for this purpose”. “Contrary to the agreed-upon coordination, the participants acted deceptively and manipulatively, without authorisation, departing entirely from the appr­o­ved framework, and began demolishing one of the monuments in Madama,” it added. It said soldiers reported the incident to their commanders, who told them to stop the activity and “the participants were quickly escorted out of the village”. In a statement, Prime Minister Benjamin Netan­yahu said the military “is the sovereign authority in Judea and Samaria”, using the Biblical term for the occupied West Bank. “Taking the law into one’s own hands, especially when it involves public figures, is a reprehensible practice that prevents the IDF from focusing on its missions of combatting terrorism and incitement to violence,” he added. Israel raids UNRWA training centre Meanwhile, Israeli for­ces began evicting a vocational training centre run by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees in an east Jerusalem suburb on Tuesday, in its latest move targeting the beleaguered organisation. It follows repeated warnings by UNRWA that Israeli authorities were threatening its Qalandia training centre, located between the east Jerusalem neighbourhood of Kafr Aqab and the Qalandia refugee camp. The centre was established in 1952 and offers vocational training to around 340 Palestinians from the occupied West Bank every year, according to UNRWA. (left) Zvi Sukkot, a member of the Israeli Knesset, smashes a monument at Madama, in the occupied West Bank; while (right) journalists react after inhaling tear gas during a raid by Israeli forces on a UN-run vocational training centre near Ramallah.—AFP “In accordance with my directive and following the law we passed, today the evacuation of the UNRWA compound in Kafr Aqab in Jerusalem has begun,” a statement from Netanyahu’s office said. Israel has repeatedly accused UNRWA of providing cover for Hamas fighters, claiming that some of its employees took part in the group’s Oct 7, 2023 attack. Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, on Tuesday celebrated “making history!” “Large forces of the Israel police are operating together with the relevant bodies to implement the law and remove UNRWA from the site,” he said on Telegram. He later posted a photo of the Israeli flag hoisted above the entrance to the training centre with the caption: “UNRWA in our hands.” An AFP journalist at the scene on Tuesday said Israeli forces had closed the main road near the entrance to the Qalandia Training Centre, while forces inside the institute were moving from one building to another. The journalist reported seeing a convoy of three civilian vehicles leaving the institute, escorted by Israeli forces. West Bank settlers attack journalists Separately, Israeli settlers in the West Bank on Tuesday attacked journalists reporting on tension with Palestinians, in violence that left at least five people injured, the reporters and medics said. A three-person team from the AFP news agency had travelled to the village of Jannatah near Bethlehem to report on Israeli activists who conduct solidarity visits with Palestinians facing harassment by Israeli settlers, who recently blocked a road in the area. After an altercation broke out between the settlers and activists, the Israeli military ordered journalists to leave what it called a “closed military zone”, at which point two additional cars full of settlers swooped in. The settlers, many of them children, threw stones towards the journalists and activists. One journalist ducked a stone but then a child settler struck him in the chin with a stick, causing minor bleeding, he said. The AFP journalists returned to see their two parked cars both damaged, with back windshields smashed in and tyres punctured. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

Montado sobre un caballo, sonríe a la cámara. Estaba de vacaciones y la guerra en la que su país se había embarcado meses antes al invadir Ucrania parecía ajena a él, pese a ser capitán del Ejército ruso. Sin embargo, el 13 de febrero de 2024, un año y cinco meses después, Kuzminov era asesinado a tiros en el aparcamiento subterráneo de una urbanización de Villajoyosa (Alicante, 37.500 habitantes) por un hecho que, precisamente, había protagonizado durante este conflicto: desertar. Hoy, aquella fotografía sigue accesible en Instagram y acumula cerca de 3.700 comentarios. La inmensa mayoría, para alegrarse de su fallecimiento. Seguir leyendo

items.title: De Guadagnino a Cuarón a Tati, cinco películas para cerrar el verano
items.description: El buen cine de verano es el que recoge sus diminutos placeres, pero el mejor es el que trata, además, su final; la despedida de ese concreto estado de desconexión, disponibilidad para la curiosidad y el hallazgo y calor. Estas cinco películas hablan de ello, cada una a su manera, y ayudan a afrontar la transición de nuestro relajado yo estival a la dura y angulosa rutina. 'Haz lo que debas'. Spike Lee, 1989 El tropo “personajes al límite durante una ola de calor” dominó la ficción americana entre los cincuenta y los setenta, de Tennessee Williams a 'West Side Story', de 'Tarde de perros' a 'Chinatown': vacas gordas para la manga corta. Spike Lee lo resucitó en los ochenta con más fuerza que nunca. Bajo un sol granítico, este duro drama tiene tanta vida, euforia y pasión que parece que, sí, así es como se sobrevive a agosto. 'Las vacaciones del Sr. Hulot'. Jacques Tati, 1953 Si hace falta excusa para regresar a Hulot, aquí una: el final (ojo, espóiler) (la película tiene 73 años, también te digo) es quizá el fin de verano más poderoso del cine, con esa inmediata nostalgia de algo que aún no hemos terminado de vivir, guinda de una obra maestra sobre el placer de descansar (en un hotel, aquí) cuando la oportunidad de hacerlo es tan finita y el deseo tan eterno. 'El cuchillo en el agua'. Roman Polanski, 1962 ¿Qué siente usted rodeado solo de agua? ¿Paz? ¿Terror? ¿Calentón? Roman Polanski investigó todas las caras de la más veraniega de las estampas en su ópera prima. Influencia directa en 'El talento de Mr. Ripley', sucede casi exclusivamente en un velero y contiene tantas emociones (y encuadres brillantes y disgustos para sus protagonistas) que, cuando acaba, ya no queda nada por idealizar de los últimos meses. 'Y tu mamá también'. Alfonso Cuarón, 2001 Desoyendo a Žižek, que decía que lo importante en esta 'horny road movie' era la alegoría política, podemos ver aquí el cénit del género “el verano nos desinhibió y ahora sé quién realmente soy”, junto a 'Casi famosos', 'El viaje de Chihiro' o 'Extraño río': alegorías sobre el PRI aparte, la película nos permite recordar, mejor que la mayoría, el gusto que da dejarse llevar cuando no hay motivo para resistirse. 'Cegados por el sol'. Luca Guadagnino, 2015 Cuando el cineasta más sensible a las luces, ritmos y placeres del verano ('Call Me By Your Name', 'We Are Who We Are') hizo su primera exhibición de fuerza, en este 'remake' de 'La piscina', de Jacques Deray, probó que el cine vacacional es más sensación que información; más atmósfera que trama. Aquí, la atmósfera está compuesta de todos los elementos perfectos: extranjeros con pudientes en entornos rurales, tensión sexual mal resuelta y esa duda posveraniega de cuánto de lo que creímos sentir nos acompañará a casa. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ángel Ortiz, el nieto del inventor de las palas de playa, quiere revolucionar este deporte
items.description: Clop, cataclop, cataclop, ¡Pi! Cataclop, clop, cataclop , ¡Boom! Clop, clop, cataclop, ¡Fium! Clop, cataclop, clop, ¡Meeec! El acostumbrado rebotar de pelotas a modo de un galope impulsado por palas de madera que resuena en las playas de Santander ha incorporado unos nuevos sonidos tecnológicos. Los históricos castañazos, décadas tronando en esos arenales del Sardinero o del Camello, han evolucionado y ahora hay un radar analizando el nivel del bombardeo. Un grupo de aficionados pretende que el juego de las palas se convierta en un deporte oficial y han incorporado a este territorio un sistema inventado en Grecia, que mide la velocidad, el total de golpes y las veces que la bola besa la arena, para ponderar el grado de esfuerzo y aptitud. Su impulsor, Ángel Ortiz, es el nieto del primer santanderino que creó esas raquetas de madera que hoy son tan populares . “Estoy llevando a cabo su sueño”, explica, aunque a los puristas no les convenza esta innovación en un juego que consiste en que la pelota no se caiga, pese a zurrarla a ritmos extremos, y que los revolucionarios buscan hacer más competitivo aplicando datos objetivos. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Robles indigna al resto del Gobierno al chocar con Marlaska y plantear que el CNI sí avisó de que venía un gran salto en Ceuta
items.description: La ministra de Defensa, Margarita Robles, generó este martes un malestar notable en el resto del Gobierno, especialmente en el núcleo más cercano a Pedro Sánchez, al chocar con el responsable de Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska. Ambos protagonizaron una evidente guerra de versiones que los ciudadanos pudieron seguir en directo en dos comparecencias casi simultáneas en el Congreso y en La Moncloa. Robles sostuvo varias veces desde el Congreso que el CNI, que tiene 25 agentes desplegados en Ceuta según desveló, sí avisó de que había mucho movimiento en la frontera con riesgo de que hubiera un salto masivo, algo que finalmente se produjo de forma inédita, con 80.000 personas en dos días. Y Marlaska, que era quien habría tenido que poner medidas si hubiera conocido las dimensiones de lo que venía, la contradijo radicalmente: “No había ningún informe que atisbara que el 30 de julio iba a acontecer lo que sucedió. ¿Alguien puede entender que si se hubiera vislumbrado algo así, con lo que pasó en 2021 [otro salto de 10.000 personas] no se habría elevado al nivel de las más altas instancias para tomar medidas extraordinarias?“, apuntó. El mensaje de Marlaska era muy claro: mientras Robles intentaba pasarle la responsabilidad a él o a la delegación del Gobierno por no actuar pese a que tenía informes alertando ―después explicó que fueron ”verbales"― el ministro del Interior fue rotundo: nadie avisó. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El encargo del Gobierno de Ayuso a la inmobiliaria de lujo que vendió el ático: “Entre 250 y 400 metros y una gran terraza”
items.description: Las instrucciones eran claras: se buscaba ático de lujo por Chamberí o alrededores . Entre enero y marzo, un mes antes de la adquisición por parte de la empresa pública Planifica Madrid del polémico ático , el Gobierno de Isabel Díaz Ayuso ya buscaba pisos que tuvieran, de entrada, las siguientes características: “Entre 250 y 400 metros cuadrados y una gran terraza”. Así lo han confirmado a EL PAÍS fuentes cercanas a la operación. Son detalles muy parecidos a los del ático que la empresa pública terminó comprando finalmente por 6,3 millones de euros y que cuenta con 485 metros cuadrados y casi 200 metros de terraza. La vivienda se anunciaba en las redes sociales de la inmobiliaria desde el 31 de enero por 6,6 y, antes incluso, en su portfolio. En ese momento fue cuando un alto cargo de Planifica Madrid contactó con la exclusiva inmobiliaria de lujo afincada en La Moraleja a través de un anuncio en internet, detallan estas mismas fuentes. La agencia les mostró al menos dos propiedades. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El hijo del burgalés desaparecido en el Mediterráneo: “Queremos que le busquen; es muy difícil, pero tenemos esperanzas”
items.description: Sergio Mutilba aún está interiorizando que su padre ha desaparecido en el mar Mediterráneo. Juan José Mutilba, de 66 años, cayó al agua desde su barco, Theorema , hace una semana . Su madre, pareja de este empresario burgalés jubilado, solo pudo alertar a las autoridades tres días después, pues quedó a la deriva y sin cobertura tras no lograr ayudar a su esposo, a quien perdió de vista en una vasta extensión marina entre Italia y Grecia. La familia suma días de tensión y ruega atención para movilizar medios en la búsqueda del hombre, conscientes de la complejidad de la operación, pero instando a destinar recursos para ellos. Su hijo apunta a que el barco era nuevo y que quizá su madre no supo manejarlo para detenerlo y rescatar a Juan José. Él muestra todavía fe: “Queremos que le busquen; es muy difícil, pero tenemos esperanzas”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Escándalo en las letras inglesas: Rachel Cusk destruye sin nombrarla a la actriz Natalie Portman en su última novela
items.description: La ficción literaria se monta con retazos de realidad. La construcción psicológica de los personajes toma siempre algo o mucho prestado de las personas de carne y hueso. El escándalo surge cuando la copia es evidente. Evelyn Waugh imaginó en Retorno a Brideshead al arribista Rex Mottram, esposo de Lady Julia Flyte, a partir de Brendan Bracken, el ministro de Churchill cuya pomposidad y vanidad detestaba el escritor. Truman Capote fue condenado al ostracismo social y a la depresión cuando reveló los secretos de “los cisnes” , las socialités neoyorquinas cuya amistad cultivó, en Plegarias Atendidas . Seguir leyendo

items.title: ‘Farmear’ aura, el fenómeno que conquista a Rosalía y espanta a mileniales y ‘boomers’
items.description: En los últimos días es probable que usted haya oído un concepto: farmear aura . Si no pertenece a la generación Z y ha visto alguno de los vídeos que ilustran esta tendencia, es muy posible que la primera reacción haya sido de desconcierto. En estos encuentros, los participantes se reúnen en el espacio público para competir entre sí con poses, gestos, piruetas y miradas basadas en el repertorio de lo viral y el meme. El objetivo es ser ingenioso, lograr guiños reconocibles y, en cierto modo, sorprender al contrincante. Pero aun así, hay que verlo para entenderlo. Y eso fue lo que hicieron Rosalía y Loli Bahía cuando, durante su reciente estancia en México, se acercaron a curiosear una de estas batallas y, por supuesto, fueron captadas por las cámaras de los asistentes. items.title: Carmody Grey, la filósofa que dijo no a Anthropic: “Cada vez estamos más solos y somos más tontos”
items.description: Anthropic contactó con la teóloga y filósofa Carmody Grey (Londres, 43 años), profesora de la Universidad Radboud (Países Bajos). La compañía creadora del chatbot Claude quería invitarla a San Francisco para participar en algo llamado “colaboración de investigación con las tradiciones de sabiduría” para “orientar la formación moral de los sistemas de IA”. Después de varias conversaciones, Grey dijo que no. Su decisión sorprendió a sus colegas. ¿Qué pequeño humano dice que no a estos gigantes que pretenden dominar el mundo? Grey lo contó en un largo ensayo en el Financial Times. Pero lo que a ella le parece más importante no es su decisión sobre Anthropic, sino la conquista mundial aparentemente imparable de la IA. “Quiero hablar del usuario, de la adicción y la deshumanización, sobre nuevas formas de violencia y explotación”, dice Grey. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ella Rubin, la actriz de 24 años que todos comparan con Julia Roberts y que triunfa con ‘Sterling Point’
items.description: Hay rostros que parecen familiares antes incluso de que sepamos dónde los hemos visto. Es lo que está ocurriendo con Ella Rubin , la actriz que interpreta a Annie Jacobson, la protagonista de Sterling Point , el nuevo fenómeno adolescente de Prime Video. La serie, estrenada a principios de este mes, se ha convertido en uno de los grandes acontecimientos del verano, alabada tanto por la prensa especializada como por un público que parece haber encontrado en ella una representación especialmente afinada de una generación , la Z, representada hasta ahora con una brocha demasiado gorda en la ficción. Y su protagonista es uno de los ingredientes fundamentales de ese éxito. Tanto es así que ha despertado un debate viral en redes sobre su parecido con otras estrellas que también fueron, como lo es ahora esta joven de 24 años, novias de América . Que si la sonrisa de Julia Roberts , que si el perfil de Anne Hathaway —ella incluso interpretó a su hija en La idea de ti —, que si esa belleza de ecos noventeros que recuerda a Winona Ryder o Rachel Weisz . La creadora de la serie, Megan Park , definió así su magnetismo incontestable: “Es imposible no sentir algo mientras la miras. Sé que un día va a ser una de las mayores estrellas del cine del mundo”. Pero hay algo mucho más interesante detrás de este nuevo rostro viral: Ella Rubin no acaba de llegar a Hollywood. Lleva más de una década preparándose para este momento. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Lo que España aún le debe a Ceuta
items.description: Me enamoré de Ceuta nada más bajar del ferri, la primera vez que viajé a la ciudad. Llevaba en la mochila y en la cabeza un revoltijo de prejuicios y lecturas —militarismos varios, novelas de la guerra de Marruecos, mucha bibliografía sobre el Marruecos colonial…— que se me fueron diluyendo en el agua del Estrecho y ya no existían cuando desembarqué y enfilé mis pasos hacia el Baluarte de los Mallorquines. Descubrí una ciudad bella y compleja, abierta al mar y a toda la rosa de los vientos, que lo mismo se muestra provinciana y tediosa un domingo por la tarde en el Revellín, que cosmopolita y vibrante como el barrio más vanguardista de una metrópoli. Unos cuantos viajes después, ya rendido sin condiciones, Ceuta me inspiró un libro sobre fronteras que cuento entre mis trabajos más queridos. Seguir leyendo

items.description: Oigo en un boletín local de la Cadena SER el martes 18 de agosto que se está acusando a una empresa de “vertir aguas contaminadas” a un estanque. items.title: Las ‘kellys’ de los hoteles denuncian que el trabajo les cuesta la salud: “Comenzamos el día con café, seguimos con Nolotil y acabamos con relajantes musculares”
items.description: Maria del Mar Jiménez, presidenta de Las Kellys de Madrid, la agrupación en la capital de camareras de piso de los hoteles , ha viajado esta semana a Barcelona pero no precisamente para hacer turismo. “Yo no quiero que estas mujeres terminen como yo, incapacitada para trabajar, con cuatro hernias discales, quistes de Tarlov en el coxis de agacharme y levantarme, los dos metacarpianos de las manos hechos polvo, dolores en el hombro y en el codo”, dice en la concentración anual que el colectivo celebró este martes por la tarde. Cada 25 de agosto desde hace 12 años, las kellys (como les gusta denominarse, en un juego de palabras por “las que limpian”) de toda España protestan por sus condiciones laborales . Y apenas ha habido avances. Denuncian el impacto de su trabajo en la salud y que las condiciones han empeorado en las útimas décadas, cuando los hoteles dejaron de contratarlas directamente y contaron primero con Empresas de Trabajo Temporal y luego con empresas de servicios: una fórmula para esquivar el convenio de hostelería e incluirlas en el de la limpieza. La diferencia salarial, destacan, es de entre 600 y 800 euros. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ‘El ser querido’: incontestable talento expresivo, escasa emoción
items.description: Espectadores no prevenidos de El ser querido podrían sospechar después de un rato de proyección que el argumento de esta película es similar al de la triunfante noruega (prescindible para mí) Valor sentimental. A saber. Ambas están centradas en reputados directores de cine que contratan a sus hijas, con las que no tuvieron relación desde hace demasiado tiempo, para que protagonicen su próxima, y tal vez definitiva, película. No es pecado, aunque sí un poco embarazoso para el que llegó más tarde, que a distintos guionistas se les haya ocurrido el mismo argumento. Pero los espectadores también constatarán que cada una es de su padre y de su madre, que se puede abordar el mismo tema con distinto desarrollo y variantes, aunque imagino el susto de los guionistas Isabel Peña y Rodrigo Sorogoyen y de los productores de El ser querido al enterarse de la iniciativa de los nórdicos, que además consiguieron el Oscar a la mejor película internacional y no sé cuántas distinciones más. Seguir leyendo El ser querido Dirección: Rodrigo Sorogoyen. Intérpretes: Javier Bardem, Victoria Luengo, Raúl Arévalo, Melina Matthews, Marina Foïs, Raúl Prieto. Género: drama. España, 2026. Duración: 135 minutos. Estreno: 26 de agosto.

items.title: AC Milan : à 15 ans, le Marocain Akram Jadid s’entraîne déjà avec les professionnels
items.description: À seulement 15 ans, le jeune Marocain Akram Jadid vient de franchir une nouvelle étape dans sa progression avec l’AC Milan en étant invité à participer à des entraînements avec l’équipe première du club lombard. Né en 2011, l’attaquant évolue régulièrement dans des catégories supérieures à son âge chez les Rossoneri. Il a notamment déjà évolué avec les U17 et s’est illustré la saison dernière en contribuant au sacre de l’équipe milanaise en championnat U15. Doté d’un profil offensif particulièrement prometteur, Jadid se distingue par sa puissance, son explosivité, ses qualités dans le dribble et son efficacité devant le but. Selon Afrik-Foot, le jeune joueur aurait inscrit près de 700 buts dans les catégories de jeunes de l’AC Milan, un chiffre qui témoigne de sa précocité. Cette première immersion avec les professionnels constitue ainsi une étape importante dans son développement, même si elle ne préjuge évidemment pas de la suite de sa carrière. Le parallèle avec Hachim Mastour La précocité de Jadid rappelle forcément le parcours de Hachim Mastour, autre jeune talent italo-marocain révélé très tôt par l’AC Milan. À l’âge de 15 ans, Mastour avait lui aussi intégré les entraînements de l’équipe première avant de signer son premier contrat professionnel à 16 ans. À l’époque, ses vidéos techniques avaient fait le tour du monde et suscité l’intérêt de plusieurs grands clubs européens. Le Maroc avait finalement réussi à le convaincre de rejoindre sa sélection nationale. Mastour avait honoré sa seule cape internationale en 2015 face à la Libye. La suite de son parcours n’a toutefois pas répondu aux attentes placées en lui. Des expériences à Malaga et au PEC Zwolle, notamment, n’ont pas permis au joueur de confirmer les immenses espoirs suscités par ses débuts. Jadid déjà partagé entre le Maroc et l’Italie Akram Jadid possède lui aussi la double nationalité. Fils de Rachid Jadid, ancien joueur installé en Italie depuis 1991, il a été entièrement formé dans le football italien, tout en ayant déjà choisi de représenter le Maroc U16. Le jeune attaquant compte actuellement deux apparitions avec les Lionceaux U16, tandis que l’Italie suivrait également attentivement son évolution. À 15 ans, il reste naturellement trop tôt pour établir des comparaisons définitives ou prédire la trajectoire du jeune joueur. Mais son passage précoce avec les professionnels de l’AC Milan confirme qu’Akram Jadid fait déjà partie des jeunes talents marocains à suivre de près. The post AC Milan : à 15 ans, le Marocain Akram Jadid s’entraîne déjà avec les professionnels appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Pakistan Agricultural Research Council suspends officers over ‘recruitment irregularities’
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Pakistan Agricultural Research Council (PARC) has suspended several officers over their alleged involvement in irregularities in the organisation’s recruitment process, senior officials of the Ministry of National Food Security and Research informed a Senate committee on Tuesday. The officials told the Senate Standing Committee on National Food Security and Research that an inquiry under the Efficiency and Disciplinary Rules had also been initiated against the officers. The committee was further informed that the matter was currently sub judice. The meeting, chaired by Senator Syed Masroor Ahsan, was attended by Senator Poonjo Bheel and Senator Sardar Al Haj Muhammad Umer Gorgaij. The committee expressed serious concern over the failure to submit the required written reply and relevant record concerning the alleged recruitment irregularities. Members also discussed the plight of candidates who had applied for PARC vacancies but were now approaching the upper age limit. The committee recommended exploring a mechanism that would allow such candidates to participate in future PARC recruitment drives even if they subsequently exceed the prescribed age limit, in order to protect their interests. Members also stressed that the prescribed provincial quota must be implemented across all posts, including lower-grade positions. Officials said the required codal formalities for implementing the provincial quota had been completed and assured the committee that the quota would be enforced. The committee was also briefed on the National Oilseed Policy and the country’s growing edible oil import bill. Officials said the federal government was planning measures to increase domestic oilseed production, with particular emphasis on olive cultivation. Senator Ahsan expressed concern over the challenges confronting domestic edible oil production and called for practical steps to boost local output. He directed the ministry to submit a comprehensive report covering progress made over the past three years, PSDP projects, initiatives related to olive oil production and future plans to increase domestic oilseed production.­ Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Who controls the answer?
items.description: A NOTIFICATION appeared on some iPhones carrying the BBC News logo. Luigi Mangione, the man accused of killing UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson in New York, had shot himself, it said. Except he had not. Mangione was alive and in custody. The BBC had published no such claim. Apple Intelligence grouped three BBC notifications into a single summary and turned one into a false statement. Following complaints from the BBC and other news organisations, Apple temporarily suspended notification summaries for news and entertainment apps. The incident was widely treated as another AI error, but its implications went further. The BBC had done the reporting, yet AI had changed what potentially millions of users thought it had reported. Its name remained on the alert even though it no longer controlled the information attached to it. Something similar is now happening on a much larger scale. People are turning to AI assistants with questions they once asked Google, journalists or experts, such as what happened in an election or why a war began. In all fairness, search engines were never neutral to begin with. They decided whether a report from Dawn appeared beside an obscure Indian website presenting itself as a research platform, and most users rarely moved beyond the first few results. But users could still open the original reports, see where each claim came from and judge the sources. AI removes that step. It reads the material, summarises it and presents its own version of what happened. This matters because malicious actors are already polluting the information space. Elections bring coordinated disinformation, synthetic audio and manipulated videos designed to promote candidates or discredit opponents. Governments and parties are no longer simply responding to news but producing their own version of events. People are turning to AI assistants with questions they once asked Google, journalists or experts, such as what happened in an election or why a war began. The same contest is visible in Gaza, where restrictions on journalists, competing claims and loaded language have shaped coverage. The killing of civilians, destruction of hospitals and homes, restrictions on aid and wider Israeli abuses are extensively documented, yet presented through radically different frames. Months of reporting by journalists, UN agencies and human rights groups may be placed against a single denial from the Israeli or US government. An AI assistant may then present both as equally credible, without showing how much evidence supports each account. The history of occupation may disappear, leaving what appears to be a dispute between two sides. The democratic danger is not limited to hallucination. It lies in allowing a handful of private companies to organise public knowledge. Citizens may receive one answer without knowing which newsroom established the facts, what evidence supports them or which accounts were left out. A confident summary can close a debate before the reader knows one exists. This is already happening. A study coordinated by the European Broadcasting Union and led by the BBC examined more than 3,000 responses from four major AI assistants across 18 countries and 14 languages. It found that 45 per cent had at least one significant issue. Serious sourcing problems appeared in 31pc, while 20pc contained major accuracy issues. There is an economic consequence too. Traditional search normally preserved the click. Readers reached the news website, encountered the original reporting and generated some advertising or subscription value. AI systems can extract the result of that work, compress it into a paragraph and retain the user. Pew found that users were almost half as likely to click on a search result when an AI summary appeared. Publishers surveyed by the Reuters Institute expect search traffic to fall by 43pc over the next three years. Their reporting is still being used, but fewer readers are reaching the organisations that produced it. Large international publishers are negotiating licensing agreements with AI companies but smaller organisations have little comparable leverage. This is particularly dangerous for Pakistan, where journalism is already weakened by declining revenues, political pressure, delayed salaries and dependence on government and corporate advertising. Most publishers have no subscription base, limited technical capacity and little understanding of how often AI systems collect their work. The European Union has begun addressing parts of the problem. Its AI Act requires certain AI-generated or manipulated material, including deepfakes and unedited text on matters of public interest, to be labelled. Providers of general-purpose AI models must maintain copyright compliance policies and publish summaries of their training material. Systems designed to influence elections are treated as high risk, while the Digital Services Act requires the largest platforms and search engines to address risks to elections and civic discourse. But these protections do not settle the central question. They do not require an assistant to present several credible accounts, explain why it preferred one source, direct users prominently to the original report or compensate the publisher whose journalism supplied the answer. Pakistan needs to begin this discussion before the terms are set elsewhere. News organisations should measure AI crawling and referral traffic, decide how their archives may be used and bargain collectively with technology companies. Common agreements should require clear attribution, links to original reports, a process for correcting false summaries and fair payment when journalism is used commercially. Publishers must also rebuild direct relationships with audiences through memberships, newsletters and products that do not depend entirely on platforms. Journalism has lost audiences to new technologies before. This time, AI does not only decide which report is seen. It can rewrite the report, mix it with weaker sources and deliver the result without the reader reaching the newsroom. If these systems depend on reporting, they cannot be allowed to make the reporter disappear. The writer is the founder of Media Matters for Democracy. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Constituency issues dominate NA session
items.description: • Deputy speaker defers entire 58-point agenda, including 20 private members’ bills • PPP legislator demands policy statement from PM on new provinces • MNAs voice concern over rise in violence against women ISLAMABAD: It was a largely non-productive and wasteful day in the National Assembly on Tuesday as lawmakers spent nearly three hours raising petty issues, mostly related to their constituencies, under the guise of “points of order”. Deputy Speaker Ghulam Shah showed great generosity by allowing more than three dozen members to speak on issues of their choice, after announcing that the day’s entire legislative agenda had been deferred under an agreement. The deputy speaker, however, didn’t elaborate on where and with whom the understanding had been reached. Later, Aliya Kamran of the opposition Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam (JUI-F) complained that her party was not consulted at all. The deputy speaker deferred the entire 58-point agenda, which included 20 private members’ bills. The House, however, took up the two calling attention notices — one related to the high fees and charges being collected by private medical colleges and the other regarding persistent river erosion in Layyah district — besides unanimously passing a resolution to mark Eid Miladun Nabi. Under the assembly rules, a member may raise a ‘point of order’ only to point out some violations during the proceedings and generally, the chair doesn’t allow the members to raise irrelevant issues under points of order. Taking advantage of the free rein given by the chair, the members spoke on all kinds of issues, ranging from matters of national importance to the problems relating to their constituencies. Interestingly, no government representative was there to respond to or take note of the points raised by the members. Most of the issues highlighted by the lawmakers were related to the provincial governments or the local governments that were not functioning. PTI lawmakers also talked about their constituency issues, but after protesting against the government’s alleged failure to implement the Supreme Court’s verdict regarding medical check-up of former prime minister Imran Khan at Shifa International Hospital, Islamabad. The speeches of the opposition members were completely blacked out on the official social media accounts of the National Assembly. Injustice to Sindh Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan and PPP legislators mostly criticised the federal government over long and frequent power outages in Karachi and other parts of Sindh. Another PPP MNA Sharmila Faruqui highlighted the alleged contradiction in the federal government’s development priorities, stating that while “the government repeatedly cites lack of fiscal space, it has approved Rs49bn in federal financing for the first phase of Lahore-Sahiwal-Bahawalnagar Motorway.” On the other hand, she said, the government had released only Rs30bn for the long-delayed strategic Hyderabad-Sukkur Motor­way, terming it a great injustice to the Sindh province. Highlighting some recent incidents, including the murder of Hina Javed in Rawalpindi, some lawmakers expressed serious concerns over the increase in violence against women in the country. Babar Nawaz and Shaista Khan of the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) referring to the murder of five-year-old Ayat Noor in Haripur, lashed out at the PTI-led provincial government, questioning the alleged silence of Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and other party MPAs over the incident. The MNAs asked the KP government to take notice of the incident and bring the culprits to justice. New provinces PPP lawmaker Agha Rafiullah demanded that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif should come to the House to give a policy statement on the issue of new provinces. Referring to a statement by Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, the PPP MNA from Karachi alleged that a cabinet member had charge-sheeted his own government by declaring that the system had collapsed in the country. On the other hand, PML-N lawmaker Babar Nawaz said the people of Hazara didn’t want to live under the present set-up and they wanted to have a separate province. He also claimed that historically, Hazara, Chitral and Swat had never been part of KP. The National Assembly will now meet on Friday at 11am. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Pakistan sits on $7tr mineral trove, claims planning minister
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has claimed that Pakistan estimates its mineral endowment at more than $7 trillion. Mr Iqbal made these remarks in a conversation with Farwa Amin, director for South Asian initiatives at the Asia Society Policy Institute in New York, as per a statement issued by the planning ministry on Tuesday. The minister said large-scale mining operations required heavy up-front investments and extensive gestation periods, and the country’s volatile political climate was a primary deterrent to international resource developers. He said that with improved macroeconomic stability, the government was actively courting foreign partners, including US firms, through mechanisms such as the memorandum of understanding with US Strategic Metals, potential EXIM financing and participation in critical-minerals ministerial processes. Indus Water Treaty Mr Iqbal said India unilaterally held the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, describing it as the “first instance” in modern history of water being weaponised and creating a serious new security challenge for Pakistan. He said the 70-year-old treaty had remained “untouchable” even through multiple wars between the two countries. He warned that India could now deny Pakistan water when it was needed for crops and release it when it was not required, turning a shared resource into a potential instrument of pressure. He said Pakistan was accelerating construction of new reservoirs to create a strategic buffer, adding that the Diamer-Bhasha and Mohmand dams, once completed, would add roughly six million acre-feet of storage capacity. These projects are intended both to stabilise water supply against climate-driven variability and to reduce vulnerability to upstream manipulation, he said, adding that Islamabad was pursuing diplomatic channels to prevent the dispute from escalating into conflict. He also placed geoeconomics at the centre of Pakistan’s foreign policy under the “Uraan Pakistan” framework and the 5E strategy, arguing that the relationship with the United States in particular must move beyond the traditional security-geopolitics axis. Ties with US, China Mr Iqbal was equally clear that en­­gagement with the US would not come at the expense of China. He described China as a “trusted partner” that stepped in during Pakistan’s energy crisis with the first phase of the CPEC, delivering approximately $25 billion in investment that ended prolonged power shortages and upgraded highways, fibre-optic networks and Gwadar Port. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Fresh efforts at mediation revive hopes for US-Iran climbdown
items.description: COMMERCIAL vessels are seen in the Strait of Hormuz, near the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas, as Tehran and Muscat agreed on a phased arrangement for the troubled waterway. According to the two sides, the agreement covers the formation of a temporary joint navigation corridor, mine clearance, information exchange and traffic management.—Reuters • Back-to-back Tehran trips by CDF Munir, Omani FM yield progress on key issues • Despite public brinkmanship, Washington ‘ready to show flexibility’ on economic sanctions if Iran meets ‘certain conditions’, US media reports • Diplomatic sources point to ‘softer than expected’ sanctions, say Islamabad taking the lead in conveying messages from Tehran to Washington, and vice versa • Iran seeks return to terms agreed in Islamabad MoU; eyes Hormuz agreement with Oman ISLAMABAD / WASHINGTON: Progress made during two key visits to Tehran — by Pakistan’s Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir and Omani Foreign Minister Badr Al-Busaidi — may have opened the first potentially workable pathway towards de-escalation in the Gulf, since the breakdown of the armistice secured through the Islamabad Memor­andum of Understanding (MoU). Although there has been no clear breakthrough yet, and fundamental differences persist between Iran and the United States, the latest diplomatic activity has brought the political and technical dimensions of the dispute back into focus. In Washington too, there seems to be a willingness to consider sanctions relief as part of a broa­der understanding with Tehran, provided Iran meets certain conditions. According to some US media reports, Washington has offered an end to economic sanctions and the naval blockade against Iran in exchange for Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz to shipping and halting attacks by Iran-aligned regional groups. However, the specific terms have not been publicly confirmed by Washington or Tehran. Importantly, unlike the period following the collapse of the June understanding, when the two sides were largely talking past each other and the crisis was bec­o­ming increasingly militarised, there is a renewed push towards establishing a new mechanism for maintaining the ceasefire. Observers believe Field Mars­hal Munir’s visit served to reopen channels bet­w­­een Tehran and Washington, through Islamabad. It is also noteworthy that the Iranian reaction to the visit was unusually positive, with Seyed Mehdi Tabatabaei, deputy for communications and information at the Iranian president’s office, describing it as “highly fruitful” and saying it had produced “highly valuable diplomatic achievements”. The CDF’s meeting with Gen Mohsen Rezaei — the Supreme Leader’s representative on the Supreme National Security Council – was particularly significant in testing whether the security side in Tehran was also prepared to join the renewed process. Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), too, said the Iranian leadership appreciated Pakistan’s “constructive role and sincere efforts” for dialogue and de-escalation. But Tehran has so far not publicly indicated any readiness to make unilateral concessions to US, rather, the message emerging from the meetings was that Iran remains prepared to return to the understanding formalised under Islamabad MoU, provided Washington first addresses what Tehran considers its violations of the memorandum, and returns to implementing the understanding. ‘Softer than expected’ sanctions Diplomatic sources in Washington also confirmed that Pakistan’s mediation role is being supported from the top, with Field Marshal Munir remaining in touch with both President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, complemented by working-level contacts between US and Pakistani officials. Asked whether Pakistan had conveyed any US proposals to Iran, sources confirmed that this was the case, adding that Tehran’s proposals have also been relayed to Washington, “along with their comments”. “So, they are not only facilitating but also [carrying out] mediation, which includes conveying their opinions as well,” sources said. The description is broadly consistent with reporting by CBS News and The Wall Street Journal , both of which have identified Pakistan as an important conduit between Washington and Tehran. As evidence of the impact this messaging is having on the Trump adm­in­­istration’s actions, diplomatic sources in Washin­gton pointed to the recent announcement of economic sanctions against Iran. Although the Trump administration had billed the sanctions as spelling an “ economic doomsday” for Tehran, diplomatic sources said: “The restrictions are softer than expected, and also, on the other side, there have been no recent attacks on Gulf states”. While the Treasury Department has announced new sanctions on 60 individuals, entities and vessels, but the list did not feature any of the Chinese financial institutions thought to be facilitating Iran’s oil trade. The Iranian position, nevertheless, remains conditional as it continues to regard the Islamabad MoU as the appropriate framework, but wants Washington to demonstrate through concrete action that it is prepared to honour its commitments. The dispute over Hormuz is, meanwhile, not being treated by Iran as a separate maritime issue rather it has been tied to the issues of sanctions, the US naval blockade and reciprocal implementation of the June understanding. Hormuz progress In this context, the progress made in Oman-Iran talks assumes greater significance. Al-Busaidi’s visit to Tehran produced some forward movement on navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, with the two sides agreeing on a phased arrangement. As per the joint statement, the understanding between Oman and Iran includes a temporary joint navigation corridor, mine clearance, information exchange and traffic management, while technical discussions would continue on a permanent navigation arrangement. Al-Busaidi said in a post on X after the meeting that he hoped the countries would “soon announce” the temporary corridor in the strait. “Future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course,” he said. Technical negotiations will continue to determine a “permanent navigational corridor and future administration of the Strait, as well as a mechanism for information-sharing, traffic management, and the provision of relevant navigational and security services”, the earlier joint statement read. The announcement came as US President Donald Trump repeated claims on Truth Social that “all mines have been removed and/or detonated from within the International Waters of the Strait of Hormuz”, citing the US navy. “Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed… There is a Zero Tolerance policy on mine placement in full force and effect,” he added. Meanwhile, the Reuters news agency reported that Washington is beginning to send personnel back to some diplomatic missions in the Middle East that were evacuated or downsized amid tensions with Iran. The move suggests Washington sees a lower risk of the conflict with Iran escalating in the near term, though some embassies will initially operate below full capacity. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Govt increases petrol price by Rs1.12, high-speed diesel by Rs1.11
items.description: Pakistan fuel prices, 2026 Official ex-depot prices (PKR/litre) — OGRA & Ministry of Energy notifications Petrol (MS-92) Diesel (HSD) Pre-crisis baseline Source: OGRA / Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division); Dawn.com · "> The government on Tuesday raised the price of petrol by Rs1.12 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs1.11 per litre. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs343.10 per litre while HSD will cost Rs371.80 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to a Petroleum Division notification, the new prices will be applicable on Aug 26 (Wednesday) and 27 (Thursday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

items.title: France permanently closes consulate in Karachi
items.description: KARACHI: The Consulate General of France in Karachi is closing its doors permanently after 50 years of service. This was announced by the outgoing French Ambassador to Pakistan Nicolas Galey at a farewell organised by the Board of Management of the Quaid-i-Azam House Museum in collaboration with the Karachi Council of Foreign Relations on Tuesday. The event was aimed at saying goodbye to two great friends of Pakistan: Ambassador Galey and the Consul General of France in Karachi Alexis Chahtahtinsky. The ambassador said that he was also feeling a bit sad after spending almost five years in Pakistan. Farewell held for French Ambassador Nicolas Galey and Consul General Alexis Chahtahtinsky “And my leaving is also coinciding with the departure of our Consul General in Karachi Alexis Chahtahtinsky. Someone will replace me in Islamabad but here in Karachi, the French Consulate, which opened in 1976, is closing down after 50 years of service,” he said. “I have visited Karachi many times and have seen the vitality of this city. I have seen it changing and improving,” he said, while appreciating Consul General Alexis for his good work in Karachi. “Even though the consulate is closing, there is still the Alliance Francaise, which will now serve as our flagship. There will also be the Pakistan France Business Alliance here doing its work,” the Ambassador reminded. He also said that he really appreciates Pakistan’s efforts in at least getting “a kind of ceasefire in the Gulf. Pakistan has emerged as a very influential country in difficult circumstances.” Consul General Chahtahtinsky said that he was leaving Karachi and Pakistan on September 1. “I am going back to France but I am taking great memories of Karachi with me,” he said, adding that he is not just a great friend but also an old friend of Pakistan. “I first visited Pakistan as a student in 1983, which was a great thing, because as a diplomat you don’t get so much freedom to go where you want. I was lucky enough to visit and fall in love with the Northern Areas of Pakistan at the time,” he said. “As the Consul General, I spent another four memorable years in Karachi, which was the first capital of Pakistan and still its economic hub. Indeed, Karachi, as the biggest port in the country, is the gateway to Pakistan,” he said. “It is a great place for doing business and has a great social life. I will always have a special place in my heart for Karachi,” he added. “Earlier Pakistan had a reputation of crime and terrorism and embassy people used to be afraid to come here. But since February 28, when the major conflict erupted in the Gulf, Pakistan has also emerged on the world map due to its mediation efforts. The entire world is grateful to Pakistan for its role. It is a very different Pakistan that we are leaving. Instead of being a problem, Pakistan has repositioned itself to become part of the solution,” the consul general said. During his vote of thanks, Vice Chairman of the Board of Management of the Karachi Council of Foreign Relations Ikram Sehgal recounted that France was the first non-Muslim nation to recognise Pakistan though diplomatic relations between both countries were established in 1951. “France has lent Pakistan support whenever we needed it. We got Daphne-class submarines followed by the Agosta-class submarines at a time when no one was giving us weapons. “Before that we had the Mirage III and Mirage 5 fighter jets. Through Project Retrofit of Strike Element [ROSE], a modernisation programme for ageing Mirage jets carried out at the Pakistan Aeronautical Complex in Kamra, we are still flying their upgraded versions. In between, we also captured some French army tanks used by India to put into use ourselves,” he said, adding that France is wrong in closing its consulate in Karachi at this time when Pakistan’s waters are turning into a major power. “This is a time when France could have taken advantage of the opportunities coming up here in the name of trade and new alliances are coming up geopolitically as Pakistan gets ready to play a big role,” he concluded. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: Indepe­ndent power producers found overcharging users through costly coal procurement
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Indepe­ndent power producers (IPPs) operating on impor­ted coal have been found imposing an additional burden on electricity consumers through opaque and inefficient coal procurement practices, with the cost ultimately passed on through monthly fuel price adjustments (FPAs). While consumer groups have been raising concerns over such practices at various forums, including public hearings, the power division and the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) have now also pointed to inefficiencies in coal procurement and their financial impact on consumers. The issue gained prominence after recent competitive bidding for coal supply to the 660MW state-owned Jamshoro Power Plant attracted a discount of $7.12 per tonne from a Karachi-based supplier compared to discounts of only 20 to 50 cents per tonne in some contracts involving IPPs. “The power division has identified significant inefficiencies in the procurement of imported coal by power plants,” an official statement said on Tuesday, adding that fresh policy guidelines had been iss­ued “for corrective action that could save the natio­nal exchequer up to Rs380 million annually”. In a recent order, Nepra had already pointed out concerns over coal procurement by Port Qasim Electric Power Company (PQEPC) under a six-year contract involving discounts of $0.20 to $0.50 per tonne based on estimated coal prices. “This type of evaluation has never been observed in any bidding by any other power plant, including PQEPC, and does not seem justified, as it is based on estimated coal prices, which may change in future,” Nepra said in its judgement. The regulator also noted that the Port Qasim plant had published its tender notice only in China instead of reaching out to a broader pool of potential bidders. “Had discounts been incorporated into the bid evaluation as a major criterion, it may have yielded more competitive and higher discounts from prospective bidders,” Nepra said. The regulator also observed that the plant had not disclosed that it had already executed a long-term coal supply agreement when the matter was discussed with the regulator on two occasions, prompting “proceedings regarding misstatement and/or non-disclosure of information”. Nepra subsequently directed the Port Qasim plant to conduct fresh bidding for a long-term coal supply agreement within three months of its March 2026 FPA decision. However, officials said that after the March 25 order, the company procured about 1.2 million tonnes of coal, enough for almost an entire year, just before a new tender. They said the contract again involved a discount of around $0.50 per tonne against the $7.12 discount secured by the public-sector Jamshoro plant. The difference alone works out to around $8 million, officials said. If similar procurement practices were followed by other IPPs, the impact could rise substantially. The power division said the procurement inefficiencies were identified during a series of meetings presided over by the power minister, where officials reviewed actual data, contractual arrangements and market practices. “Pakistan has a significant fleet of coal-fired power plants with a combined capacity of approximately 5,280 megawatts that rely wholly or partly on imported coal. These include three major 1,320MW plants at Port Qasim, Hub Power and Sahiwal, as well as the Lucky and Jamshoro plants which also have the capability to use imported coal,” it said. The division said coal import prices for IPPs were linked to internationally recognised benchmarks such as the API-4 index, but the final price paid by a plant also depended on the discount negotiated with the supplier. PQEPC Chief Financial Officer Adil Ashraf and Procurement Chief Liang Ding Ping did not respond to Dawn’s written queries. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

items.title: How close are humanoid robots to becoming part of our everyday life?
items.description: At the ongoing 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games, multiple robots have clocked times better than human benchmarks in sprint and other track‑and‑field events, marking rapid progress in humanoid‑robot technologies. Industry observers on site note that while competitions showcase the cutting‑edge technical capacity of today's robots, real‑world everyday applications remain in the early phase. Robots are gradually moving beyond exhibition‑only competition demos toward practical deployment in real‑life scenarios. One industry participant at the games pointed out that this edition brings notable new milestones. For the first time, robot competitive results are measured against human performance benchmarks, proving robots can outperform humans under specific controlled conditions. Unlike earlier competitions that largely focused on basic locomotion, this year's event features a wide range of autonomous operation challenges — an important step toward broader industrial adoption. Still, competition‑level performance does not automatically translate into viable mass‑market consumer products. Pain points and limits uncovered during matches can drive further technical iteration. Meanwhile, non‑humanoid robotic alternatives, such as wheeled platforms fitted with robotic grippers, also hold considerable practical application potential. Kang Yu, general manager of the Capital Markets Department at Shoucheng Holdings, shared her observations on industry investment trends. Against a backdrop of surging investor interest in robotics, many industry players are prioritizing long‑term foundational‑technology R&D rather than chasing short‑term market hype. Investment spans multiple links across the robotics value chain: robot hardware, joint materials, embodied‑intelligence models, computing infrastructure and data. A key focus lies in boosting product reliability and consistency, with further improvements expected to come as production scales up. The public listing of Unitree Robotics represents a meaningful capital‑market turning point for the sector. It highlights value‑driven technology as a core underpinning for the industry's long‑term growth outlook. Experts tracking real‑world robot deployment said physical‑world testing spaces in Beijing's commercial districts, transport hubs and office complexes now display over 200 types of intelligent hardware, with use‑cases covering home companionship, education and healthcare. Industry projections suggest robot costs could drop substantially over the next three years. As algorithms keep advancing, robots may eventually evolve into mass‑consumer goods. Deploying robots within real‑world use‑cases will be central to how the industry moves forward.

items.title: France : une tornade fait une quarantaine de blessés et endommage 300 habitations
items.description: Une tornade d’une rare intensité a fait une quarantaine de blessés, dont deux en urgence absolue, et endommagé quelque 300 habitations, lundi à Pomas, village de l’Aude, dans le sud-ouest de la France, rapportent mardi les médias locaux, citant les autorités. Au lendemain du phénomène météorologique, les opérations de reconnaissance et de sécurisation se poursuivaient dans cette commune d’environ 1.000 habitants située dans le massif des Corbières, où d’importants dégâts matériels ont été constatés. Selon la préfecture de l’Aude, citée notamment par l’AFP, 75 sapeurs-pompiers étaient mobilisés mardi pour poursuivre les opérations de vérification, tandis qu’un audit des bâtiments était engagé afin d’identifier d’éventuelles fragilités structurelles et les risques d’effondrement. Les habitations endommagées doivent également faire l’objet d’opérations de bâchage, alors que plusieurs routes demeuraient interdites à la circulation et qu’environ 1.400 foyers étaient encore privés d’électricité mardi matin. Les images diffusées par les médias français témoignent de la violence du phénomène : toitures arrachées, maisons fortement endommagées et débris projetés dans les champs et les rues du village. Les secours ont travaillé durant toute la nuit et des sinistrés ont été accueillis dans la salle polyvalente de Pomas, avec l’appui de la Croix-Rouge. D’autres ont été relogés chez des proches ou dans des communes voisines. La tornade avait frappé Pomas lundi en fin d’après-midi, alors que plusieurs départements du sud-ouest de la France avaient été placés en vigilance orange aux orages par Météo-France, qui avait alerté sur la possibilité de phénomènes localement violents. Selon Météo-France, la France connaît en moyenne quelques dizaines de tornades chaque année, avec des intensités variables. L’organisme souligne toutefois que l’influence du changement climatique sur la fréquence, l’intensité et la répartition géographique de ces phénomènes demeure à ce stade incertaine. The post France : une tornade fait une quarantaine de blessés et endommage 300 habitations appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: 'Not an enemy:' Slovakia calls on EU for 'friendly' China competition
items.description: Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said on Tuesday that the European Union (EU) should pursue "friendly" competition with China rather than treat the country as an enemy and put up barriers. Fico made the remarks after talks in Bratislava with European Council President Antonio Costa, who began his annual tour of EU capitals in Slovakia. Fico said Slovakia was concerned about the EU's ability to compete globally, arguing that greater competitiveness should not mean imposing new tariffs or barriers, but rather striving to do better and outperform others. "I have a different view about relations between the EU and China. I don't think we should fight China by putting up barriers and treating it as an enemy," Fico said. "China is a country with which we should compete in a friendly spirit and strive to do better." The two leaders' discussions also covered the EU's next long-term budget, competitiveness, energy prices and enlargement. On the EU budget, Fico said Slovakia supported maintaining a strong cohesion policy to reduce regional disparities across the bloc. "We're even saying that some extra funding should be found for countries in the eastern part of the EU, which, for example, share borders with Ukraine," he said, adding that a strong agricultural policy is another key Slovak priority. On an EU enlargement, Fico reiterated Slovakia's support for countries seeking membership, adding that all applicants must meet the required criteria. "That means no exceptions and no shortcuts. And that also applies to Ukraine," he stressed. Fico said Ukraine should not be allowed to overtake countries such as Montenegro, Albania or Serbia in the accession process, arguing that they had been preparing for EU membership for much longer. (With input from Xinhua)
